latestRelease.notes:
# Hermes Agent v0.20.3 (v2026.8.16.2)

**Release Date:** August 16, 2026

> Patch release. This tag rolls up the ~125 PRs merged since v0.20.2 into a stable tagged release for downstream consumers (Docker images, hosted deployments, fresh installs).

---

## About this release

Since v0.20.2 (v2026.8.16, tagged earlier today), this window landed **~250 commits** across **~461 files** (+42,613 / −1,641) — **~125 merged PRs** including the MCP 2.x SDK migration and 2026-07-28 stateless protocol support, the bundled Bot Mode (hermes-bots) plugin with the core teammate protocol, the CommandCode provider plugin, subprocess Python runtime ownership hardening (PYTHONHOME/PYTHONPATH isolation), Cua Driver 0.20 runtime contracts for computer use, kanban worktree/dispatch fixes, cron continuity flags, desktop remote-gateway headers and connection self-healing, cron scheduler self-heal (EMFILE recovery, stale-claim reconciliation, wedged-job re-arm), session handoff data-loss fixes, plus a wave of ports from the ecosystem scout slate (plugin install security scanning, /worktree, /rollback hand-edit preservation, UTF-16 file reads, Gemini 3 tool-call ID preservation, and more).

**Full curated release notes for this window will ship with v0.21.0**, which will document everything from v0.20.0 onward — highlights, feature areas, and complete contributor credits. Nothing in this window is skipped.

## Updating

- `hermes update` from an existing install
- Fresh install: `curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/main/scripts/install.sh | bash`

**Full Changelog**: https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/compare/v2026.8.16...v2026.8.16.2

signals.title: fix(delegation): failed API calls consume the subagent iteration budget, starving the fallback chain
signals.text: ## Summary In subagent execution, the iteration budget is consumed **before** the model API call is made, and `api_call_count` is incremented before it too. A retryable failure — HTTP 429 → `FailoverReason.rate_limit` → `try_activate_fallback` walking `_fallback_chain` — burns the same budget as a successful turn. When a burst of rate limits coincides with a subagent deep in a long code-read (50-90 iterations in), the run can terminate with `exit_reason=max_iterations` before the configured `fallback_providers` chain gets a fair chance to recover, with the 429 as the last visible event. ## Evidence (all verified in code) - `agent/conversation_loop.py:1425` — `api_call_count += 1` happens **before** the API call. - `agent/conversation_loop.py:1433` — `elif not agent.iteration_budget.consume():` also runs **before** the call; a failed call is never refunded (no `refund()` call on error paths). - `agent/iteration_budget.py:37-45` — `consume()`/`refund()` exist; `refund` is not invoked on API failure. - `agent/chat_completion_helpers.py:1695-1757` — `try_activate_fallback` walks `_fallback_chain` on `FailoverReason.rate_limit` / `billing` / `upstream_rate_limit`. - `agent/error_classifier.py:33` — `rate_limit = "rate_limit" # 429 or quota-based throttling — backoff then rotate`. - `agent/agent_init.py:1390-1398` — `_fallback_chain` populated from `fallback_providers` (list) / `fallback_model` (dict); subagents inherit it via `tools/delegate_tool.py:1463` → `fallback_model=parent_fallback` → `run_agent.py` child construction. - `tools/delegate_tool.py:1352-1355` — per-subagent iteration cap, default 50 (config currently 200). ## Observed manifestation Ten red-team subagents were dispatched to audit the secrets-exfiltration hardening. Six exited with `exit_reason=max_iterations` after 58-90 tool calls each, each with a terminal `HTTP 429: rate limit exceeded` after 3 retries in the transcript — despite `fallback_providers: deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash` configured and the fallback chain verified wired end-to-end. The 429s were retryable; the budget was not. The fallback chain never engaged because the subagents had exhausted their iteration budget on deep code reads, and every failed API call had consumed budget as if it were a successful turn. ## Proposed fix 1. **Refund or don't consume on API failure**: do not consume an iteration (or `refund()` it) when the API call fails with a retryable classification and the fallback chain is about to engage — a fallback attempt is part of the same logical turn, not a new iteration. 2. **Decouple retry/fallback from the turn budget**: count `api_call_count` for observability, but gate loop exit on a separate budget that excludes provider-recovery attempts, or cap recovery attempts independently (e.g. N fallback tries per logical turn). 3. **Test**: a subagent whose primary provider 429s on every call, with a healthy `fallback_providers` entry, must complete the task — not die with `max_iterations` after burning the budget on failed calls. ## Impact - Subagents on rate-limited primary providers silently fail instead of using the configured backup — the exact failure the `fallback_providers` feature exists to prevent. - Affects every delegation workload: red-team audits, research fan-outs, code reviews — anything deep enough to approach the iteration cap. ## Severity HIGH (reliability/availability; the configured resilience path is defeated by budget accounting).

signals.title: [Bug] Hermes Desktop: chat view jumps to a historical message block while the assistant is still responding
signals.text: ## Bug description In **Hermes Desktop** (the desktop app), while the assistant is still generating a reply, the chat view suddenly jumps/scrolls away to an **earlier (historical) chat block** in the conversation. The user loses sight of the current in-progress response and must scroll back down manually to continue reading it. This happens in the desktop app chat UI — not in CLI/TUI mode. ## Steps to reproduce 1. Open Hermes Desktop and start a conversation. 2. Ask a question that produces a long streaming answer. 3. While the response is still being generated (do not scroll manually), watch the viewport. 4. The chat view jumps to a historical message block from earlier in the conversation, leaving the current response out of view. ## Expected behavior The chat view stays anchored on the assistant's current streaming response until the user scrolls manually. ## Actual behavior The viewport jumps to a historical chat block mid-response. ## Environment - **Product**: Hermes Desktop (portable desktop edition) - **Desktop app version**: 0.17.0 (`apps/desktop/package.json`) - **Core version**: 0.20.0 (`pyproject.toml`) - **Build commit**: f5be9236e (built 2026-08-04, branch `main`, source `local`) - **OS**: Windows 10 Pro 10.0.19044 (22H2) - **Mode**: Desktop chat UI ## Possibly related - #69554 (feat(desktop): preserve per-session chat scroll position) — related to scroll position handling but this is about an active jump during streaming, not restoring position across sessions.

signals.title: [Feature]: Design mode — element selection bridge from desktop preview/browser pane to agent context
signals.text: ## What A "design mode" for the Hermes desktop app: click an element in the preview pane (or the in-app browser panel from #48760), and the selection is piped to the agent as structured context (tag, classes, text content, bounding box, and a best-effort source hint), so the user can say "make this button bigger" and the agent edits the right file. ## Why Cursor, Claude Code, and v0 all have some form of this loop, and it's the highest-friction gap when using Hermes for frontend work today. The agent can open a dev server in the preview pane via `open_preview` and read back page text with `read_preview`, but there's no path from "the thing I'm looking at" to "the element the agent edits." Users describe elements in prose ("the blue button near the top") and the agent greps for it. It works, but it's the slow version of the loop. ## Proposed shape 1. **Selection overlay in the preview webview**: a toggle (palette command / keybind) that highlights elements on hover and captures click selection, similar to browser devtools inspect mode. 2. **Selection → agent context**: the captured element info is attached to the user's next message (or exposed via a `read_preview_selection` tool the agent can call), riding the same gateway blocking-bridge pattern `read_terminal` and #48760's `desktop_browser_*` tools use. 3. **Source hint (best effort)**: for localhost dev servers, include `data-*` attributes or sourcemap-derived file hints when available; degrade gracefully to selector + text content when not. 4. The agent side needs no new core concepts: it receives the selection as context and uses existing file tools to make the edit, then the preview hot-reloads. ## Notes - Depends conceptually on #48760 (the browser panel) but could prototype against the existing preview pane first. - Desktop-gated (`HERMES_DESKTOP`), no impact on CLI/gateway surfaces. - I'm happy to prototype this as a desktop plugin first to validate the interaction model before proposing core changes. ## A note on authorship This issue was cowritten with my Hermes agent (running on this repo's own codebase as its reference), and I'd genuinely love to help implement it, with that same agent pairing with me on the work. Filing it first to get the team's read on direction before writing code. ## Related - #48760 (in-app browser side panel + agent control) - #68364 (agent-assisted skin builder, adjacent "agent edits live UI" territory)

signals.title: Required CI aggregate treats skipped and non-failure states as passing and excludes Docker from the gate
signals.text: <!-- security-campaign-marker: SECURITY-AUDIT-42-CLASSES-F51AA6A9 --> <!-- security-campaign-class: SECURITY-CLASS-7f244fef4359b8ad --> **Campaign interlock:** Part of [EPIC #82591](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/issues/82591). **Final class:** `SECURITY-CLASS-7f244fef4359b8ad` **Consensus contract:** `R5-C-004` # Required CI aggregate treats skipped and non-failure states as passing and excludes Docker from the gate **Consensus contract:** `R5-C-004` **Source pin:** `f51aa6a9b5ce514e15f8e337777f522fd5cc6fa2` **Route:** public hardening issue under `SECURITY.md` §3.2 **Severity:** `HIGH` ## Scope - `.github/workflows/ci.yml:190-250` (blob `6aa601e264fe854f532b72358343c55dd33e58be`) - `.github/workflows/ci.yml:107-123` (blob `6aa601e264fe854f532b72358343c55dd33e58be`) - `.github/workflows/ci.yml:219-222` (blob `6aa601e264fe854f532b72358343c55dd33e58be`) ## Defect class The confirmed source defect is the aggregate's result semantics and explicit coverage exclusions; it is not a claim that GitHub branch protection currently requires or accepts a particular check configuration. ## Current controls - Job result visibility in the summary. - Explicit workflow dependencies and timeouts. - Some empty-output paths fail closed outside this evaluator. ## Required remediation - Require result == success except for an exact, independently justified skip. - Reject cancelled/timed_out/neutral/missing/unknown states. - Separate intentional OS skips from classifier skips and make Docker/release-sensitive checks required for matching changes. ## Acceptance contract - Unit-test the evaluator for success, failure, skipped, cancelled, timed_out, neutral, missing, and unknown states; only explicit success or justified skip may pass. - Make a changed desktop path require E2E and a Docker-sensitive path require the Docker status. - Add an uncovered-change invariant and fail when any changed file maps to no lane. ## Affected files - `.github/workflows/ci.yml` - `scripts/ci/classify_changes.py` ## Godfile dependencies - `CI aggregate evaluator` - `conditional job selectors` - `branch-protection required-check contract` Any touched file above 2,000 lines must route through a separate behavior-neutral Shard before the hardening change. The security PR must not grow or restore a godfile. ## Existing graph and credit - No overlap recorded ## Interlock Part of #82591. The implementation PR must use a closing keyword for this issue, and both the issue and EPIC must link back to the exact PR. ## Evidence boundary This issue contains the independently adjudicated hardening contract, not a public exploit recipe. Exact attacker-path evidence remains in the content-addressed campaign evidence held outside the public issue.

signals.title: Default URL redaction preserves userinfo and query credentials at non-navigation-capable boundaries
signals.text: <!-- security-campaign-marker: SECURITY-AUDIT-42-CLASSES-F51AA6A9 --> <!-- security-campaign-class: SECURITY-CLASS-bf89e9b049acb1d6 --> **Campaign interlock:** Part of [EPIC #82591](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/issues/82591). **Final class:** `SECURITY-CLASS-bf89e9b049acb1d6` **Consensus contract:** `R3-C-004` # Default URL redaction preserves userinfo and query credentials at non-navigation-capable boundaries **Consensus contract:** `R3-C-004` **Source pin:** `f51aa6a9b5ce514e15f8e337777f522fd5cc6fa2` **Route:** public hardening issue under `SECURITY.md` §3.2 **Severity:** `HIGH` ## Scope - `agent/redact.py:963-992` (blob `b5dca332c4ade1cee8564a02e22f8b9d10f750b9`) - `agent/auxiliary_client.py:6253-6292` (blob `13bce3f884199c96fcfba0b760860af1b031f6c9`) ## Defect class Confirmed policy-context mismatch: navigation-safe preservation is reused at log/provider-metadata boundaries. The custom-endpoint choice itself is not adjudicated as unauthorized access; this is a public hardening route. ## Current controls - Optional strict URL redaction. - Generic known-token and database-connection-string handling. - Endpoint-specific provider headers and URL parsing. ## Required remediation - Make strict URL redaction mandatory outside a typed navigation capability. - Strip query/userinfo before base URL cache identity and provider metadata unless an explicit policy permits it. ## Acceptance contract - For every non-navigation URL log, error, dump, header, and provider metadata path, assert strict query and userinfo redaction. - Require an explicit typed navigation path for URLs whose query must remain actionable. ## Affected files - `agent/redact.py` - `agent/auxiliary_client.py` - `agent/agent_init.py` ## Godfile dependencies - `provider client construction and logging/status callers` Any touched file above 2,000 lines must route through a separate behavior-neutral Shard before the hardening change. The security PR must not grow or restore a godfile. ## Existing graph and credit - No overlap recorded ## Interlock Part of #82591. The implementation PR must use a closing keyword for this issue, and both the issue and EPIC must link back to the exact PR. ## Evidence boundary This issue contains the independently adjudicated hardening contract, not a public exploit recipe. signals.title: [Bug] Windows/Chinese file delivery & preview: garbled MEDIA filenames, artifact-tag chain broken on Windows paths, dismiss not persisted
signals.text: **Environment**: Windows 11, Hermes Agent v0.20.0 (2026.8.3, main @ f4c2c263f), Chinese locale, CJK paths (e.g. `D:\坚果云同步\工作\...`) Three related desktop-UX defects, all from **POSIX-path / ASCII-filename assumptions**. Real daily impact for Chinese/Windows users. ## 1. MEDIA attachment filename shows URL-encoded garbage for CJK paths - `mediaName()` (media.ts) uses `new URL(path).pathname` — WHATWG `URL.pathname` always percent-encodes CJK → filename displays as `%E6%B5%8B...` in the attachment card. - File opens fine; display-only defect. ASCII filenames unaffected (why English-only users never see it). - Current workaround: copy to ASCII-named path before delivery. ## 2. Composer status-stack artifact tag chain broken for Windows paths - `looksLikePath()` (targets.ts) accepts only `file://`, `/`, `./`, `~/` prefixes — `C:\...` (backslash) never matches → **no artifact tag at all** for Windows absolute paths. - macOS agents naturally write `/Users/...` → tag + IPC preview work (Claude-style artifact). Windows agents write `C:\...` → nothing. - Even with POSIX form (`/c/Users/...`), IPC `normalizePreviewTarget` resolves it to non-existent `C:\c\...` → tag appears but preview fails. - Verified 2026-08-13: `write_file(path="/c/Users/...test.html")` → tag shows, click preview fails; `write_file(path="C:\...")` → no tag. ## 3. Preview-artifact tag dismiss not persisted — tags keep returning - `dismissPreviewArtifact` (preview-status.ts) removes only from an in-memory atom; the tool row's `useEffect` re-registers on every remount (scroll / window re-open) → dismissed tags reappear. `/clear` doesn't help; only `/new` clears. - Users constantly hit this with generated HTML reports. **Expected**: (1) decode CJK filenames for display; (2) accept `C:\` absolute paths in `looksLikePath` / `localPreviewTarget` (e.g. `/^[a-zA-Z]:[\\/]/`); (3) persist dismissed-artifact state per session. **Related**: #84986 (file actions on preview links); #84375 (same POSIX-assumption class in search_files — fixed 2026-08-12, thanks).

signals.title: [Feature]: Animated desktop avatar / companion plugin — looking for feedback and contributors
signals.text: ## Problem or Use Case I have been building a working **animated avatar / desktop companion plugin for Hermes Desktop** with `@hermes/plugin-sdk`. The goal is to give Hermes a small visual character that reacts to what the agent is doing instead of remaining a static UI element. I think this could be a fun optional community plugin for Hermes users, and I would like feedback/help from maintainers and other users who are interested in improving it. ### What the prototype can do today The current prototype runs as a Hermes Desktop plugin and already supports: - IDLE animation - BLINK animation - TALK animation - expressions such as thinking, excited, curious, sad, heart, etc. - 10 dedicated action poses / states - PET interaction / pet animation - separate visual FX such as question, idea, heart, sparkle, scan, data, loading and glitch - manual buttons to test expressions and all action poses - Canvas-based fixed-cell sprite rendering to avoid visible sprite-atlas scrolling - pane + status-bar popup integration in Hermes Desktop The character atlas is currently structured as: - Row 0: IDLE × 8 - Row 1: BLINK × 6 - Row 2: TALK × 6 - Row 3: EXPRESSIONS × 12 - Row 4: ACTIONS × 10 - Row 5: PET × 8 The 10 action poses currently represent things such as: 1. Wave 2. Point 3. OK 4. Thumbs up 5. Cute / playful 6. Hug 7. Sleep 8. Processing 9. Focus 10. Agent mode ## Goal The next step is to make the avatar react reliably and automatically to Hermes state, for example: - user/STT listening → attentive/listening pose - transcription → processing/thinking - model thinking / streaming → thinking - TTS / read-aloud playback → TALK - tool execution → processing / scan - subagent/delegation activity → agent/focus mode - successful completion → OK / thumbs-up / smile - error → sad / glitch - long idle → sleep Ideally the avatar should feel like a small visual representation of what Hermes is currently doing, while remaining completely optional. ## Current technical limitation The Desktop Plugin SDK already provides useful host state and `host.onEvent()`, but this type of plugin would benefit from more stable **semantic state hooks**. Hermes Desktop internally has voice playback states such as `idle`, `preparing`, and `speaking`, but a normal disk desktop plugin should not import Desktop internals directly. For the prototype I experimented with generic gateway events and observing the rendered voice-status UI, but that is not a robust long-term integration. The same issue appears with higher-level lifecycle states: streamed gateway events are useful, but a visual companion needs a clean source of truth for states such as listening, transcribing, thinking, speaking, tool-running, finished, and error. ## Proposed Solution I would like to keep the avatar itself as a **community plugin**, rather than requiring it to be bundled into Hermes core. What would help this plugin — and potentially other visual/notification plugins — is exposing a few stable Desktop Plugin SDK signals, for example: ```ts host.state.voicePlayback // idle | preparing | speaking ``` and ideally a higher-level voice conversation state: ```ts idle | listening | transcribing | thinking | speaking ``` Other useful hooks could include: - stable tool-running / tool-finished state - subagent/delegation activity - model generation/thinking state - turn completed / failed - optional TTS activity or amplitude information for more natural mouth animation I am not attached to these exact API names — I mainly want to understand what the recommended stable integration point should be. ## Help / feedback wanted If anyone from NousResearch or the Hermes community is interested, I would especially appreciate help with: - the cleanest supported way for a Desktop plugin to react to STT/TTS state - reliable tool/subagent/model lifecycle triggers - smoother animation/state transitions - optional audio-reactive mouth animation - plugin packaging/versioning/update workflow - testing on other Hermes Desktop installations/platforms - deciding where a real community Desktop plugin should live and how users should discover/install it I already have a working prototype and can continue working on the avatar, sprite atlas, UI and testing side. ## Distribution / community plugins The Desktop Plugin SDK documentation describes disk plugins under: ```text $HERMES_HOME/desktop-plugins/<id>/plugin.js ``` as the recommended user delivery mode, which works well technically. My question is mainly **discovery**: what is the preferred way to bring a real third-party Desktop plugin to Hermes users? I found the `NousResearch/hermes-example-plugins` repository, but its README describes those plugins as intentionally small, single-surface reference examples. This avatar is becoming a real multi-surface user plugin rather than a minimal SDK example. Would the Hermes project be interested in any of the following? - a community plugin index/gallery - a documented list of third-party Desktop plugins - a separate community plugins repository - or simply recommending that real plugins live in their own GitHub repositories and are linked from discussions/docs Guidance here would be very helpful before I package/publish the prototype more broadly. ## Alternatives Considered ### Observe the Hermes Desktop DOM This can detect visible voice playback labels and is useful for prototyping, but it is brittle and should not be the permanent integration. ### Parse `host.onEvent('*')` This works for some activity, but generic streamed events can repeatedly restart animations and do not provide one authoritative high-level avatar state. ### Keep everything manual The manual test controls work, but automatic reactions are the main goal of the plugin. ### Publish only as a standalone repository This is probably the simplest immediate option, but I would like to know the recommended community distribution/discovery path first. ## Scope The avatar plugin itself can stay external/community-maintained. The Hermes-side request is mainly about **Desktop Plugin SDK state/event hooks and guidance for community plugin distribution**. If maintainers prefer, this can be split into separate issues for: 1. voice/lifecycle state hooks in the Desktop Plugin SDK 2. community Desktop plugin discovery/distribution I am happy to provide screenshots, video, the current plugin code and sprite-atlas details if useful.

signals.title: Multiplex gateway profiles share the default profile session database
signals.text: ## Bug description Multiplex gateway profiles share startup-created `SessionStore`/`SessionDB` instances rooted in the default profile. Secondary-profile turns can therefore persist transcripts to the default profile's `state.db` and discover default-profile sessions through ordinary `session_search`. ## Code evidence - `GatewayRunner` creates one startup-scoped `SessionStore`: `gateway/run.py:6584-6593`. - `SessionStore` creates its `SessionDB()` before secondary turn scope: `gateway/session.py:1238-1293`. - The runner creates another startup-scoped `SessionDB()` for agent tools at `gateway/run.py:6814-6819`. - Every multiplex agent receives that shared DB: `gateway/run.py:5498-5509`. - `session_search` uses the injected DB unless `profile=` is explicitly supplied: `tools/session_search_tool.py:978-1033`. - This conflicts with `_profile_runtime_scope`'s contract that sessions follow the profile home: `gateway/run.py:2067-2077`. ## Deterministic probe A default-profile DB containing a unique marker was injected exactly as the multiplex runner does while `HERMES_HOME` was scoped to a worker profile: ```text worker_home= .../profiles/worker injected_db= .../default/state.db hits= [('default-secret-session', '>>>DEFAULT_ONLY_MARKER<<<')] ``` The worker profile found the default-only transcript through ordinary discovery without an explicit cross-profile request. ## Expected behavior Each profile persists and searches only its own profile-local `state.db` unless the caller explicitly requests another profile through the existing cross-profile read interface. ## Actual behavior All multiplex agents receive the default profile's startup-created database. ## Impact Cross-profile transcript disclosure and incorrect transcript persistence. This violates the profile isolation boundary even when profile ContextVars are otherwise correct. ## Suggested fix Allocate a profile-local `SessionStore`/`SessionDB` per profile and inject the store selected by the active profile. In multiplex mode, ordinary `session_search` should be profile-scoped by construction. Add a two-profile regression test covering both persistence and discovery. ## Environment - Hermes Agent v0.20.1 - Audited commit: `56526bc0d36522ab7a87ee0056f70e3847d2f0e6` - Multiplex gateway with default and secondary profiles

signals.title: Cron/session recovery: fence reconciliation by exact ownership generation
signals.text: ## Summary The recent session-persistence and cron-recovery train closes several real data-loss and silent-wedge paths, but the combined architecture still has one shared correctness gap: **recovery operations are not consistently fenced against a successor owner**. The relevant fixes are individually sound for the incidents they address: - #88244 prevents CLI cleanup from finalizing a session after `/handoff` has transferred it to the gateway, and surfaces `state.db` initialization failure instead of silently degrading persistence. - #88335 stops `EMFILE`/`ENFILE` from being classified as harmless tick-lock contention and adds degraded-health/backoff behavior. - #88337 clears one-shot `run_claim` on pre-dispatch failures. - #88339 re-arms recurring jobs wedged in restart-surviving persisted error state. - #88343 reconciles stale process-local in-flight claims against the durable execution ledger. Taken together, however, these fixes reveal the next class boundary: **an old recovery actor can still clear, release, finalize, or re-arm state that now belongs to a newer generation of the same session/job.** The invariant should be: > Every attach, clear, finalize, release, or reconcile operation must identify and conditionally match the exact ownership generation it intends to mutate. A stale actor must be unable to mutate its successor. This issue tracks that class as one coherent recovery/fencing problem rather than another series of incident-local TTL guards. ## 1. `/handoff`: completion-to-cleanup still has a narrow ownership race #88244 adds the session ID to `_handed_off_session_ids` only after the CLI polls `get_handoff_state()` and observes `state == "completed"`. Cleanup suppression is therefore process-local knowledge acquired *after* the gateway has committed the handoff. There is still a legal ordering: 1. Gateway completes the handoff and assumes/reopens the session. 2. CLI has not yet observed `completed`, so its session ID is not yet in `_handed_off_session_ids`. 3. CLI receives SIGTERM / abnormal shutdown / another cleanup trigger. 4. Old CLI finalizes the session now owned by the gateway. That is the original ownership bug compressed into a smaller window. Marking the session as handed off earlier is not sufficient: a failed handoff must leave the CLI as the legitimate owner. The transfer needs a durable generation/lease or equivalent CAS boundary: ```text CLI owns session S generation A Gateway prepares generation B commit atomically transfers A -> B CLI finalize(S, expected_generation=A) succeeds only while A still owns S ``` Cleanup should be rejected by durable ownership state, not by whether this particular CLI process has learned that the transfer completed. ## 2. One-shot dispatch recovery: `clear_run_claim(job_id)` can clear a successor claim #88337 correctly adds cleanup on interpreter-shutdown, execution-creation, and executor-submit failures. But the cleanup primitive is keyed only by `job_id`: ```python def clear_run_claim(job_id: str) -> bool: ... if job.get("run_claim") is not None: job["run_claim"] = None ``` The durable `run_claim` already carries owner/timestamp information. Cleanup does not require that the stored claim still be the claim acquired by the failing attempt. ABA ordering: 1. Attempt A owns claim A. 2. A stalls. 3. A's claim expires/is reclaimed. 4. Attempt B writes claim B for the same job. 5. A resumes into a pre-dispatch failure path. 6. A calls `clear_run_claim(job_id)`. 7. Claim B is erased. B can now be executing while the durable job appears unclaimed, permitting another dispatch. The primitive should be compare-and-clear, preferably against an opaque claim ID plus owner: ```python clear_run_claim( job_id, expected_claim_id=claim_id, expected_owner=owner, ) ``` If the persisted generation changed, stale cleanup is a no-op. ## 3. In-flight ledger reconciliation should match execution identity, not `job_id + claimed_at` #88343 loads the latest execution per job and decides that a terminal row belongs to the process-local claim when its `claimed_at` is at/after `_running_since[job_id]`. That is temporal correlation, not causal identity. A different execution for the same job — manual run, another gateway/process, retry, external provider — can become the latest terminal row and satisfy the timestamp comparison. The local sweeper can then release an unrelated local claim. The inverse exists too: a newer nonterminal execution can become `latest`, hiding the terminal execution belonging to the stale local attempt and delaying recovery until the age path fires. `cron/executions.py` already gives every attempt a unique execution ID. The local running registry should retain that ID and reconcile the exact row: ```text registration_token -> job_id, execution_id, future, monotonic_started_at ``` Then ledger reconciliation is `execution_id -> terminal?`, not "latest row for this job appears new enough". Wall-clock timestamps should remain audit data; they should not be the ownership fence. Local elapsed age should use a monotonic clock. ## 4. The process-local running registry has the same ABA shape `_running_job_ids`, `_running_since`, and `_running_futures` are keyed by job ID. `release_running_job(job_id)` is idempotent but generation-blind. A stale registration can therefore mutate a successor: 1. A registers job X. 2. A stalls before attaching its real future. 3. Sweeper releases X. 4. B registers X. 5. A resumes and attaches A's future to the slot now logically owned by B. 6. A finishes and calls `release_running_job(X)`. 7. B's in-memory protection is removed. The local API needs the same token discipline as the durable claim: ```python token = try_register_running_job(job_id) attach_running_future(job_id, token, future) release_running_job(job_id, token) ``` All three operations must compare the current token. A stale actor must be unable to attach to or release a successor registration. ## 5. Persisted-error recovery needs durable liveness/disposition, not cadence inference alone #88339 detects a restart-surviving wedge from `last_status == "error"`, old `last_run_at`, future `next_run_at`, schedule cadence, and "not running in this process". It then pulls an interval job to `now`, or a cron job to the next legal occurrence. That closes the observed EAGAIN wedge, but the discriminator cannot distinguish a wedge from several legitimate states: - operator intentionally deferred `next_run_at`; - schedule changed after the failed execution; - another process currently owns/retries the job; - the error is permanently blocked (invalid config, revoked credential, missing runtime dependency) rather than retryable; - irregular/DST-sensitive cron cadence is poorly represented by a cached gap between two future occurrences. The cross-process case is the correctness boundary: "not running in this process" is not proof that no live execution exists elsewhere. Recovery should eventually be based on explicit durable state such as: ```text execution_id dispatch_generation lease_owner lease_expiry schedule_revision error_disposition = retryable | blocked | paused ``` Automatic re-arm should require proof that the exact generation has no live owner and is eligible for retry. ## 6. `state.db` degradation is now visible, but not yet self-reconciling #88244 stores the initialization error and sends best-effort recovery guidance to configured home channels. That fixes the silent-failure surface when delivery succeeds. Two remaining sides: 1. The warning itself uses delivery infrastructure that may also be unavailable. If every send fails, the failure can again exist only in logs. 2. The fallback session store is volatile. If `state.db` becomes repairable while the gateway remains alive, there is no demonstrated durable unhealthy latch + retry/reattach + replay/migration path for sessions accepted during degraded operation. At minimum, persistence health should remain durably/probe-visibly degraded until the store is successfully reopened. If volatile sessions cannot safely be migrated, they should be explicitly identified as unrecoverable rather than disappearing on restart. ## 7. `EMFILE` recovery should distinguish temporary headroom from actual healing #88335 correctly makes FD exhaustion a failed tick and retries with backoff. `gc.collect()` and raising the soft `RLIMIT_NOFILE` can create temporary headroom, but neither proves the underlying leak stopped. A live referenced FD leak survives GC; raising the soft limit can simply postpone the next failure. Health should become green only after a real tick successfully acquires the lock and completes the expected tick path. The recovery telemetry should make sustained pressure visible — current descriptor count/limit and/or growth signal if cheaply available — so a limit increase does not erase evidence of a continuing leak. ## Proposed implementation shape This does not need one giant rewrite. The class can be closed incrementally around one shared primitive: **generation-fenced ownership**. ### A. Introduce opaque ownership tokens For each mutable ownership surface: - session lifecycle/handoff generation; - one-shot `run_claim` generation; - process-local running registration token; - exact cron `execution_id`; - external `fire_claim` where not already sufficiently fenced. ### B. Make every destructive transition conditional Replace generation-blind operations with CAS-like forms: - `finalize_session(..., expected_generation=...)` - `clear_run_claim(..., expected_claim_id=...)` - `release_running_job(..., token=...)` - `attach_running_future(..., token=...)` - ledger reconciliation by exact `execution_id` - persisted-error rearm only when durable ownership/disposition proves recovery is safe. ### C. Separate clocks by purpose - monotonic time: in-process elapsed-age/TTL decisions; - durable wall-clock timestamps: audit/history/operator display; - opaque IDs/generations: ownership correctness. No correctness decision should infer ownership from wall-clock ordering when an exact identity can be carried instead. ## Required adversarial tests Please add deterministic interleaving tests, not only steady-state regression tests: - **handoff:** pause after gateway commit but before CLI observes completion; terminate CLI; old generation must not finalize the gateway-owned session; - **durable one-shot claim:** A acquires claim A, B replaces it with claim B, delayed cleanup from A must leave B untouched; - **local running registry:** sweep A, register B, then allow A to attach/release; neither stale operation may mutate B; - **execution reconciliation:** create a terminal execution for the same job in another process after the local claim began; it must not release the unrelated local attempt; - **inverse reconciliation:** newer nonterminal execution must not hide the exact stale execution being reconciled; - **persisted error:** intentionally defer a failed recurring job; automatic recovery must not pull it forward; - **cross-process persisted error:** process B holds a live durable lease while process A scans; A must not re-arm; - **persistence degradation:** all warning transports fail; degraded state remains observable; repair the DB without restart and verify the declared replay/migration policy; - **EMFILE:** keep a live FD leak through GC/limit increase; health stays degraded until an actual successful tick. ## Acceptance criteria - A stale actor cannot clear/release/finalize a newer owner of the same job/session. - Recovery decisions use exact ownership/execution identity wherever that identity exists. - No local running-set mutation is keyed solely by reusable `job_id` when generations can overlap in time. - Cross-process liveness is considered before persisted-error auto-rearm. - Persistence degradation remains observable until durable storage is actually healthy. - The above adversarial interleavings are covered by deterministic tests. ## Why keep this as one class issue The recent fixes are converging on the right semantic direction: cron/session recovery should self-reconcile instead of waiting for TTL, restart, or operator action. The next failure mode is therefore not another missing cleanup call; it is **cleanup without fencing**. Closing this class gives the recovery layer a reusable rule: recovery may revoke only the ownership generation it can prove stale. That rule composes across handoff, cron claims, execution ledger reconciliation, restart recovery, and future multi-process scheduling work.
signals.author: andrexibiza

signals.title: [Security]: Close use-time, provenance, and authority gaps behind #88232 / #88435
signals.text: ## Problem #88232 closed one concrete incident path: malformed SSH host input could retain a pasted password, reach `desktop.log`, and then escape through a public debug share. #88435 proposes a much broader ten-part hardening campaign. Several pieces are directionally valuable, but review of head `194ecf5a3c4fdb32708b9bc79759e46d03aa8b00` found a common boundary problem: > Security decisions are often made against an early representation — a script path at create time, a final pathname, an inbound allowlist, a syntactically parseable JSON file, or a wrapper entrypoint — rather than against the final actor, bytes, authority, destination, and state at use time. That leaves bypasses even when the individual guard appears correct in isolation. This issue tracks that one class across cron execution, media delivery, outbound routing, credential persistence, and support-bundle logging. It is not a request to reject all of #88435; several fixes can land independently. It is the class-closure work needed before the campaign can be treated as an end-to-end security boundary. ## Confirmed gaps ### 1. `no_agent` cron approval is not bound to the bytes that execute F3 scans a script at job creation/update. The job stores a mutable path, not an approved digest or immutable payload. A script can therefore be benign when scanned and then be edited, replaced, or symlink-swapped before a later fire. Existing persisted jobs also never pass through the new create/update scan unless they are edited. The finite content-pattern scan is defense in depth, not containment. The branch's own F4 regression deliberately constructs a config rewrite that F3 cannot recognize, proving that script behavior can diverge from the create-time verdict. Required invariant: > The exact executable object authorized for a job must be the object executed, and execution must not receive ambient authority merely because its source text avoided a pattern list. ### 2. F4 restores `config.yaml` after execution instead of preventing unauthorized use The runtime guard snapshots `config.yaml`, runs the script with ordinary subprocess authority, and restores the file after completion if the bytes changed. That leaves several race/data-integrity edges: - a transient policy flip can be observed by another thread/process while the script is still running; - a detached child can perform its first write after the parent exits, so no initial tamper detection occurs and the settle loop never starts; - the fixed 1/2/4-second settle window is not a security boundary; - a legitimate concurrent operator edit is indistinguishable from malicious script tampering and can be overwritten by restoration; - restoration failure leaves the modified security policy live. Snapshot/restore can be useful recovery telemetry, but it cannot substitute for filesystem/process isolation or a pre-execution authority check. ### 3. F3 and F6 compose into a staging bypass F6 makes known user-data locations non-deliverable while deliberately preserving temp/cache paths for agent-produced artifacts. Because the decision is based on the final pathname, denied data can be copied into an allowed staging location and then delivered. A non-secret canary reproducer is sufficient: ```sh cp "$HOME/Documents/hermes-media-canary.txt" /tmp/hermes-report.txt printf 'MEDIA:/tmp/hermes-report.txt\n' ``` The original path is denied. The copied file is accepted because provenance was discarded and `/tmp` is treated as an artifact location. The same shape applies to cache roots, operator-allowlisted roots, and fresh home-root outputs. A denylist over familiar directory names also does not cover custom data directories, external volumes, network mounts, localized folders, repositories, or organization-specific sync roots. Required invariant: > Moving or copying denied input into a trusted output directory must not silently convert it into an authorized deliverable. ### 4. Cron destination ownership is modeled from inbound authorization and enforced through incomplete doors F9 correctly identifies that raw `platform:chat_id` targets can bypass normal platform authorization. The proposed implementation then treats inbound user allowlists as evidence of outbound destination ownership. Those are different principals on several platforms: - a Discord user ID is not a Discord channel ID; - a Slack user ID is not a Slack channel ID; - an inbound wildcard or sender allowlist is not an outbound exfiltration grant. The check is also placed in `create_job_with_scheduler_registration()` and the model-tool update wrapper rather than the core `cron.jobs.create_job()` / `update_job()` mutation primitives. Direct callers, plugins, migrations, persisted-store edits, and old jobs can therefore bypass the policy. Finally, validation occurs at create/update time only. Removing a target from an allowlist later does not revoke an already-persisted job. Required invariant: > Outbound authority must be represented explicitly and revalidated at fire time against connection × profile × platform × chat/thread identity. ### 5. Corrupt-auth handling still fails open on structural and truncation states F10 raises for malformed JSON/UTF-8, but an existing zero-byte or whitespace-only `auth.json` is treated as a legitimate empty store. Syntactically valid but structurally invalid data also falls back to a new empty provider store. Examples that must not be silently interpreted as an intentional empty credential store: ```json [] ``` ```json {} ``` ```json {"provider": {"nous": "..."}} ``` A crash-truncated file, an unsupported schema version, a mistyped top-level key, and an intentionally initialized empty store are materially different states. Conflating them recreates the read-empty/write-empty credential-erasure path F10 is intended to close. ### 6. Windows credential-write failure policy is inconsistent The Claude credential writer refuses persistence and deletes the new file when ACL restriction cannot be enforced. Hermes' own `auth.json` writer instead keeps the written credential store and logs a warning when Windows ACL enforcement fails. Therefore the advertised invariant — refuse-and-delete when a credential file cannot be restricted — is not class-wide. The behavior depends on which credential path wrote the secret. The Windows verification helper also parses localized `icacls` display text. Native-Windows tests must prove both positive ownership recognition and rejection of unrelated explicit/inherited ACEs; a parser that simply fails to identify an ACE must not return success. ### 7. The merged SSH fix closes the reproduced path, not the final support-bundle sink #88232 correctly rejects the exact `host:PASSWORD` incident shape and adds defensive target redaction. Residual compositions remain worth pinning: - comma-mangled host plus a colon secret can hit the comma error branch before the secret-hiding branch; - a colon-containing credential can be only partially masked by a one-segment regex; - IPv6 and credential-position parsing share colon syntax; - rejected raw connection input should never be interpolated back into errors or lifecycle logs; - the debug-share/public-paste boundary still needs a final whole-payload secret scrub, independent of upstream parser correctness. The durable class closure is structured safe logging plus a final egress scrub, not an indefinitely growing family of SSH-target regular expressions. ## Interlocks ### Direct - #88232 — merged incident-path repair for SSH host validation and logging. - #88435 — proposed ten-part hardening campaign reviewed here. - #82936 — cross-profile ambient-secret inheritance into subprocesses; directly relevant to what a cron script process receives. - #88335, #88337, #88339, #88343 — current cron recovery semantics that any rebase and execution-time guard must preserve. ### Related but separately owned - #82010 — explicit zero-tool state and empty toolsets failing open. This issue does not duplicate that acceptance matrix. - #88698 — MCP dual-era protocol correctness/conformance. This issue does not own protocol negotiation or cache conformance. ## Acceptance criteria ### Cron executable identity and containment - [ ] A job persists an immutable script payload or a cryptographic identity for the approved bytes. - [ ] Fire-time execution verifies that identity immediately before spawn; changed/replaced/symlink-swapped scripts fail closed. - [ ] Existing persisted `no_agent` jobs are reconciled/migrated rather than grandfathered around the new boundary. - [ ] Script execution receives an explicit capability envelope for filesystem, environment, network, and child-process access; ambient gateway/profile secrets are not inherited by default. - [ ] `config.yaml`, auth stores, pairing state, and other control-plane files cannot be transiently modified by the script lane. - [ ] A concurrent legitimate operator edit is never overwritten by a stale script-run snapshot. - [ ] Cancellation, timeout, detached-child, gateway restart, and cron recovery paths preserve the same invariant. ### Media provenance - [ ] Copying a denied canary file into temp/cache/fresh-output roots does not authorize delivery. - [ ] Trusted delivery is based on an operator grant or verifiable agent-output provenance, not only final pathname/mtime. - [ ] Every media-send path, including cron and direct gateway delivery, consumes the same final validator. - [ ] Symlink, hard-link where detectable, container-path translation, external-volume, and cross-profile cases are covered. ### Outbound destination authority - [ ] Core `create_job()` and `update_job()` enforce destination policy; wrappers cannot be the only gate. - [ ] A dedicated outbound destination grant is distinct from inbound sender authorization. - [ ] Grants are keyed by connection/profile/platform/chat/thread and cannot collide across same-named profiles or connections. - [ ] Destinations are revalidated immediately before each fire so revocation is effective for existing jobs. - [ ] Existing persisted jobs with raw targets are migrated, quarantined, or fail closed until explicitly approved. ### Credential-store integrity - [ ] Missing store, explicitly initialized empty store, zero-byte/truncated store, malformed JSON, wrong schema, and unsupported version are distinct states. - [ ] Existing zero-byte/whitespace/wrong-schema stores fail closed and cannot feed a later empty overwrite without explicit operator recovery. - [ ] Recovery copies are versioned/non-overwriting and preserve the original bytes. - [ ] Every credential write path has one documented ACL-failure policy; no path silently retains a credential that the policy says must be private. - [ ] Native Windows tests exercise localized/account-SID output, inherited and explicit group ACEs, missing current-user ACE, and enforcement failure. ### Logging and support bundles - [ ] Rejected connection input is represented by structured safe fields, never echoed raw. - [ ] Combined malformed-input cases and IPv6 are covered. - [ ] Debug-share/support-bundle generation applies a final secret scrub to the complete payload before upload/publication. - [ ] Tests use canary secrets to prove the sink does not publish material missed by an upstream parser-specific redactor. ### Integration evidence - [ ] The work is rebased onto current `main`, including the merged cron recovery train and current delivery/auth implementations. - [ ] Tests assert final composed behavior, not only intermediate helper return values. - [ ] Linux, macOS, and native Windows CI run the relevant boundary tests. - [ ] Mutation/adversarial tests prove each guard fails when removed and cannot be bypassed through a sibling entrypoint. ## Non-goals This issue does not own: - the complete MCP 1.x/2.x protocol matrix (#88698); - the complete explicit-zero-tool contract (#82010); - every possible prompt-injection defense; - a general-purpose sandbox product unrelated to the `no_agent` execution boundary. ## Closure statement This class is complete when security posture is attached to the final executable bytes, actor/profile, outbound destination, data provenance, credential-store state, and publication sink — and those facts are revalidated at the moment authority is exercised, not inferred once from an earlier string, path, wrapper, or parser result.
signals.author: andrexibiza

signals.title: Multiplex: profile identity is late-bound across transport, session, storage, and control paths
signals.text: ## Summary Hermes has accumulated profile isolation at several layers, but it still has no single point where an inbound event's profile identity becomes canonical and immutable **before the first stateful use**. A multiplexed turn can currently have several independently derived identities: 1. **transport / credential owner** — which adapter and bot/account received the event; 2. **routed runtime profile** — which profile's config, SOUL, skills, credentials and filesystem should execute it; 3. **session namespace** — `agent:main:...` versus `agent:<profile>:...`; 4. **physical persistence scope** — which `state.db`, `sessions.json`, logs and auxiliary tables hold the state; 5. **outbound transport** — which live adapter sends the reply, status, approval, typing update or callback. Those answers are currently re-derived at different times from `source.profile`, adapter ownership, transport provenance, `get_active_profile_name()`, the ambient `HERMES_HOME`, or a startup-created store/adapter map. When any one is missing or resolved too early, a single logical turn can split across profiles. The repository now has many concrete reports and PRs repairing individual faces of that same defect class. This issue is the architecture/interlock issue for closing the class rather than landing mutually inconsistent local fixes. ## Scope correction This issue does **not** depend on the claim that equal key strings in two different adapter instances automatically alias their local dictionaries. `_pending_text_batches`, `_active_sessions`, `_session_tasks` and `_post_delivery_callbacks` are adapter-instance state; two adapters each holding the string `agent:main:telegram:dm:<uid>` do not, by that fact alone, share one Python dict entry. The demonstrated defect is stronger and more general: - one adapter can derive `agent:main:...` before its event is stamped and the runner can later derive `agent:<profile>:...` for the same turn; - runner-global and durable lookups can alias profiles that share the same peer tuple; - a correctly routed runtime can persist into the wrong physical store or reply through the wrong transport; - reconstructed, callback, relay, recovery and control-command paths can omit or independently recompute the profile. Any claim of cross-adapter local-map interference should be proven with a real two-adapter behavioral test. The closure contract below does not require that claim. ## Direct interlock map ### A. Identity is established after adapter-level state/key use - #88404 / #88437 — adapter-derived session keys can be built before the per-credential profile handler stamps `source.profile`. - #49634 / #49962 — earlier Telegram manifestation combining late profile stamping and default-adapter egress. - #69156 — independently proposes stamping adapter ownership before busy/approval/session-key checks. - #85350 / #85355 — independently proposes a central `_ensure_source_profile` / `_event_session_key` seam because `/new`, `/reset`, batching and busy paths can key before normal runner ingress. - #80212 — Feishu secondary-profile events can regress to `agent:main` after runtime/reconnect/idle behavior, consistent with profile ownership being lost or rebound too late. These are not four unrelated bugs. They are competing implementations of the same missing invariant: **canonicalize identity before batching, busy state, approval state, commands or session-key construction.** ### B. Interactive and control paths rebuild incomplete identity - #82975 / #82980 — clarify lookup used an unprofiled adapter key while the runner stored the clarify under a profile-namespaced key. - #83345 / #83346 — active-session clarify replies miss the pending clarify and fall into the interrupt path because the adapter and runner use different keys. - #83889 — Feishu production manifestation of the same clarify/key split. - #86308 — Telegram slash-confirm / clarify / dangerous-command callbacks reconstructed a source without applying the routed profile before authorization. - #59018 — Matrix root-DM `/stop` needed profile-aware control-key matching. - #61012 — relay passthrough slash commands, buttons and modals were a second ingress plane that omitted profile even after ordinary relay events carried it. `/stop`, `/new`, `/reset`, clarify, approval buttons and internal redispatch are not secondary consumers. They are session-identity consumers and need the same canonical identity as normal text ingress. ### C. Transport ownership and routed runtime profile are distinct axes The repository already has both halves of this distinction: - #65236 / #65273 / #69246 — for a **shared credential**, a routed secondary runtime has no adapter of its own; egress and intake policy must preserve the receiving transport adapter. - #70620 / #70625 — for a **per-credential** deployment, a routed profile may own a distinct adapter; egress must use that profile's adapter rather than blindly preserving the receiving transport. - #79113 — the inverse route, a secondary-owned adapter routed to `default`, can produce `agent:main` while leaving the tool runtime under the adapter owner's secondary `HERMES_HOME`. - #74787 — `_adapter_for_source` is used by authorization and delivery even though those call sites have opposite fallback requirements. - #87830 — WhatsApp routed-turn authorization demonstrates the same owner/runtime conflation: config belongs to the receiving adapter while `source.profile` names the routed runtime. `source.profile` cannot safely mean both “which profile executes” and “which credential/transport owns this event.” A correct implementation needs both pieces of information and an explicit selection policy for shared-credential and per-credential topologies. ### D. Durable identity, lineage and recovery are independently derived - #74285 — peer fallback omits profile, allowing identical Telegram DM tuples to adopt a sibling profile's session and execute its persona/tools/credentials. - #74153, #74593, #75043 and #85205 — overlapping lookup fences for that report. - #88381 / #88387 — cross-profile adoption can then propagate through parent inheritance and durably mislabel descendants even when the `session_key` remains correct. - #58032 / #58119 / #58136 / #59325 — toggling multiplexing can recover stale rows from another profile namespace. - #75198 — combines profile-scoped peer recovery with another unscoped state key (`/voice`). The durable layer must consume canonical identity. It must not reconstruct profile ownership from a peer tuple that is intentionally identical across bot credentials. ### E. Physical storage policy is currently contradictory This is a merge-blocking architectural interlock: - #87240 describes the multiplexer's **shared session store** as the intended design and changes session listing/detail to read the shared store with profile filters. - #66887, #87723 and #88532 report secondary-profile sessions physically landing in the root/default store as an isolation failure. - #69042 and current #88632 implement the opposite policy: resolve/cache a `SessionDB` per active profile home so secondary writes land in `profiles/<name>/state.db`. Those approaches are mutually exclusive unless the read/write architecture is made explicit. If #87240's reader assumes a shared multiplexer store while #88632 moves writes into per-profile stores, list/detail can diverge in the opposite direction: the reader looks in the shared store while the writer has moved elsewhere. Before either model lands as repository truth, the project needs one declared invariant: - **shared physical store:** every writer uses one store and every reader/filter/API treats `session_key`/`profile_name` as the partition key; or - **per-profile physical stores:** every writer resolves the profile store and aggregation explicitly opens all served profile stores. The current mixture supports neither invariant reliably. ### F. Profile identity is lost on alternate ingress and async boundaries - #60586 — ordinary relay wire events had to carry `profile` explicitly. - #61012 — passthrough interactions required the same change separately. - #68332 — built-in Signal lacked the runner back-reference required to apply `profile_routes` at source construction. - #80956 — A2A request threads lose profile ContextVars; the proposed fix captures immutable adapter-owned security context at startup. - #56508 — import-time path resolution can freeze one profile's hooks directory for every later profile. - #70858 — pairing generation writes the default store while authorization reads the routed profile store. These are the same temporal failure pattern outside session keys: ownership is known at one boundary, discarded, then later inferred from ambient process state. ## Root cause The multiplexer currently treats profile identity as a value that downstream consumers may rediscover rather than as provenance that must be carried. Contributing design problems: 1. `None` is overloaded to mean both **known default profile** and **profile unresolved/not installed**. 2. `source.profile` is overloaded as both logical runtime routing and adapter/credential ownership. 3. Key construction is a free function used directly by adapters and subsystems, so callers can omit the profile or choose different fallback rules. 4. Some stateful objects (`SessionStore`, `SessionDB`, caches, path constants) bind to the ambient profile at construction/import time, before per-turn scope exists. 5. Interactive, synthetic, relay and recovery paths rebuild `SessionSource` independently and do not all preserve the same provenance. 6. Authorization and delivery share adapter-resolution helpers despite requiring different fail-closed/fallback behavior. ## Required invariants for class closure ### 1. Canonical identity before stateful use Before any of the following occurs, Hermes must have one canonical identity for the event: - text/photo/media batching; - active/busy session guards and pending-message queues; - `/stop`, `/new`, `/reset`, clarify and approval/callback resolution; - internal `gateway_session_key` validation and redispatch; - session lookup, creation, recovery, reset and parent inheritance; - physical store selection; - status/progress/typing/final response delivery. A frozen `SessionIdentity`/`RoutingIdentity` value object would make the contract explicit, but the exact API is open. It should at minimum carry: - transport binding / receiving adapter provenance; - credential-owner profile or account identity; - routed runtime profile; - normalized session namespace; - persistence scope/store identity. ### 2. `default` must be explicit internally Known ownership by the default profile should remain the string/value `default` internally. `None` should mean absent or unresolved. The serializer may still emit legacy `agent:main:...` byte-for-byte. In multiplex mode, an unresolved identity at a stateful boundary should fail closed or be deterministically resolved at the canonicalization seam. It should not silently become default ownership. ### 3. Separate transport owner from runtime profile The routing decision matrix needs to be explicit: | Topology | Runtime/profile state | Intake policy | Egress transport | |---|---|---|---| | Per-credential profile, no route override | credential owner | owner adapter | owner adapter | | Shared credential routed to secondary | routed profile | receiving transport owner | receiving transport | | Per-credential source routed to another profile that owns an adapter | routed profile | receiving transport policy unless explicitly delegated | declared routed adapter policy | | Secondary-owned transport routed to `default` | default | receiving transport policy | receiving transport unless product policy says otherwise | | Restored/synthetic source with no live provenance | stored runtime profile | fail closed unless an explicit binding can be resolved | fail closed; never guess another bot | The exact product choice for the two route-override rows should be documented and tested. What must not happen is accidental selection by whichever field a helper happens to inspect first. ### 4. One session-key construction seam Adapter and plugin code should not call the free `build_session_key(source, ...)` path directly with optional/omitted profile semantics. A gateway/adapter-owned constructor should consume the canonical identity. Add a repository test or lint check preventing new adapter-level direct key construction outside the canonical module/seam. Otherwise this class will recur with the next platform adapter. ### 5. One storage model Resolve the #87240 versus #88632 policy conflict before merging both assumptions. Whichever model is selected must make these agree: - session key namespace; - `profile_name` column; - physical DB path; - `sessions.json` / routing index; - list/count/detail/search APIs; - parent lineage; - topic/voice/auxiliary state. ### 6. Canonical identity survives every boundary Serialization/reconstruction must preserve the necessary fields across: - relay ordinary events and passthrough interactions; - inline callbacks; - held-inbound redispatch and reconnect; - internal events, Kanban wakeups and webhook/API ingress; - session recovery and restart; - thread/executor boundaries where ContextVars do not propagate. Ambient `get_active_profile_name()` or process-global environment must be fallback-only when no canonical identity exists, never an override of carried provenance. ## Acceptance matrix Class closure needs composed behavioral tests, not only helper-string tests. ### Per-credential collision case Two profiles, two Telegram bot tokens, the same human DMing both bots (`chat.id == user.id`): - distinct canonical session namespaces; - no cross-profile session adoption or parent inheritance; - correct physical persistence according to the selected storage model; - correct bot for progress, typing, approval, streamed and final replies; - `/stop`, `/new`, `/reset`, clarify and approval on bot A cannot affect bot B; - reconnect and idle eviction do not erase adapter ownership. ### Shared-credential routed case One live adapter, route one chat/thread to a secondary profile: - runtime/config/SOUL/tools/session namespace are secondary; - intake policy and egress use the shared receiving transport; - no requirement for a secondary adapter registry entry; - callbacks and synthetic/internal events preserve the routed profile. ### Secondary-to-default inverse case A secondary-owned adapter with a route target of `default`: - session key is legacy `agent:main:...`; - runtime `HERMES_HOME`, credentials and tools are default; - transport provenance remains explicit and egress follows the documented policy; - persistence lands in the store selected for default under the chosen storage architecture. ### Recovery and alternate ingress Run the same assertions after: - gateway restart; - routing-index miss / conservative peer fallback; - idle-TTL eviction; - adapter reconnect; - relay normal event and passthrough callback; - inline approval/clarify callback; - internally routed event carrying `gateway_session_key`. ### Composed-head interlocks At minimum, test the combined behavior represented by: - #88437 with #83346 — #83346 deliberately assumes the adapter busy key stays `agent:main`; #88437 changes that premise. - #88437 with #85355/#69156 — choose or reconcile the competing ingress canonicalization mechanisms rather than stacking duplicate state. - #88387 with the selected peer-fallback implementation and storage model. - #87240 with #88632 — do not merge contradictory reader/writer storage assumptions. - #69246 with #70625 — shared transport and per-credential override must both remain correct. ## Existing-data repair Forward-only fixes are insufficient for deployments that already crossed profiles. Add a dry-run + repair path that can detect and optionally repair: - `session_key` namespace versus `profile_name` mismatch; - rows physically stored in a DB inconsistent with the selected storage model; - cross-namespace `parent_session_id` links; - duplicate/cross-profile `gateway_routing` entries; - profile-less Telegram topic/voice rows; - stale `sessions.json` entries that re-seed wrong routing on boot. The repair should report every proposed move/update before mutation and preserve a backup/rollback artifact. ## Architectural precedent #67455's multi-account Telegram design states the useful invariant directly: account identity is stamped on the source and key construction reads it from the source so the adapter guard and session store cannot derive different identities for the same event. Multiplex profiles need the same construction, generalized to transport owner + routed runtime profile rather than one overloaded field. ## Non-goals - This is not a request to merge every linked PR. - This does not require changing the public legacy `agent:main` key format. - This does not claim every profile-scoped config/cache bug belongs in one implementation PR. - This does not choose shared-store versus per-profile-store policy; it requires that the repository choose one and make readers/writers consistent. ## Proposed disposition of current work 1. Treat #88437, #85355 and #69156 as competing/overlapping ingress implementations and select one canonical seam. 2. Rebase/retest #83346 after that seam because its regression fixture encodes the old adapter-key premise. 3. Choose the physical storage model before landing both #87240 and #88632 assumptions. 4. Land one peer-fallback fence, then retain #88387's inheritance fence and add repair for existing crossed lineages. 5. Compose #69246 and #70625 into one documented transport-selection matrix. 6. Add the end-to-end matrix above before declaring the multiplex profile-isolation class closed.

signals.title: i18n: hardcoded English strings in hermes-bots plugin and intro copy don't respect locale
signals.text: ## Summary Some user-facing strings in the desktop app are hardcoded in English and don't go through the i18n system, so they stay in English regardless of the selected locale. ## Where I found them **1. `hermes-bots` bundled plugin (`apps/desktop/src/plugins/hermes-bots/plugin.js`)** Roughly 150 user-visible strings, including the most prominent surfaces of the app: - Bots roster: `BOTS`, `Search bots…`, `New Agent`, `No conversations yet — say hi` - Cronjobs: `Cronjobs are recurring tasks this agent runs on a schedule.`, `Create Cronjob`, `Every hour / week / month`, etc. - Agent creation / edit flows, group chats, avatar generation, error toasts **2. Rotating intro copy (`apps/desktop/src/components/chat/intro-copy.jsonl`)** 75 headline/body pairs shown on the new-session screen, e.g. "Search the repo, edit files, run tests, open PRs. Tell me the goal and I'll handle the mechanical parts." **3. Misc core strings**, e.g. `NEW SESSION` in `apps/desktop/src/app/session/hooks/use-prompt-actions/resolve-target-session.ts` ## Suggestion The kanban plugin already establishes a nice pattern for plugin-scoped i18n (`ctx.i18n.register` + `usePluginI18n('kanban')` in `apps/desktop/src/plugins/kanban/i18n.ts`). Would you be open to migrating the `hermes-bots` plugin strings to the same mechanism, so each locale can register its own bundle? The intro-copy.jsonl case is less obvious — it's rotating editorial content rather than UI labels, so it may deserve its own treatment (e.g. per-locale content files, or an i18n key per entry). ## Contribution offer I'd be happy to help with the extraction and to provide the Simplified Chinese (and Traditional Chinese) translations once the strings are keyed. Just let me know if the approach sounds reasonable, or if you'd prefer a different structure — happy to discuss and follow whatever convention you prefer. (Related: I also sent a small PR completing the missing `zh` keybind strings, and noticed `zh-hant.ts` is missing ~541 keys — glad to work on that too if useful.)

signals.title: Desktop Bot Mode misclassifies active remote profiles as local and duplicates rows
signals.text: ## Summary After a v2 remote connection is successfully opened, Bot Mode can render the active remote source's profiles as though they belonged to the local source. This produces duplicate `default`/profile rows and makes the roster look like local bots have been copied into the remote view. ## Environment - Hermes Agent / backend: `v0.20.2` - Desktop source: current `main` at `4323c67dcc6048fc8e311cdff7600d3d6a17807f` - macOS arm64 - Local connection remains available, with a v2 token-authenticated remote connection configured ## Reproduction 1. Keep a local Desktop connection and configure a v2 remote connection. 2. Open a bot/profile from the remote source in Bot Mode. 3. Let the Bot Mode roster refresh. 4. Inspect the Bot Mode list. ## Actual behavior - `profiles.list` returns the active remote source's rich rows. - `mergeMultiSourceRoster()` assumes those rows are always local. - It annotates an active remote row with the local source's handle/identity when the profile name overlaps (especially `default`). - It then appends a second, thin row for the same remote agent from the union roster. - The user sees duplicated rows and local-looking `default` bots while viewing a remote source. ## Expected behavior The rich `profiles.list` rows must be associated with the currently active registry source, not assumed to be local. The remote source's profile should appear once, with its own handle and source label. Profiles from other sources should remain separately routable rows. ## Root cause `apps/desktop/src/plugins/hermes-bots/plugin.js` treats `local` in `mergeMultiSourceRoster(local, union)` as the local machine. In practice, it is the active gateway response, which may be remote after `host.ensureAgent()` activates a remote agent. The plugin also uses one static roster query key, so a remote-to-local (or local-to-remote) switch can briefly reuse the preceding source's roster response. ## Proposed fix 1. Expose the credential-free active registry connection ID through the Plugin SDK state. 2. Scope the Bot Mode roster query key by that source ID. 3. Match rich `profiles.list` rows against the active source ID while merging the union roster. 4. Do not append a thin duplicate when a rich active-source row already exists. ## Regression coverage A regression test should activate a remote source containing `default` while the local source also contains `default`, and assert that: - the remote rich row keeps its description/session data and remote handle; - only one row is emitted for that remote agent; and - the local row stays a separately routable source row.
