signal.title: Cron/session recovery: fence reconciliation by exact ownership generation
signal.text: ## Summary The recent session-persistence and cron-recovery train closes several real data-loss and silent-wedge paths, but the combined architecture still has one shared correctness gap: **recovery operations are not consistently fenced against a successor owner**. The relevant fixes are individually sound for the incidents they address: - #88244 prevents CLI cleanup from finalizing a session after `/handoff` has transferred it to the gateway, and surfaces `state.db` initialization failure instead of silently degrading persistence. - #88335 stops `EMFILE`/`ENFILE` from being classified as harmless tick-lock contention and adds degraded-health/backoff behavior. - #88337 clears one-shot `run_claim` on pre-dispatch failures. - #88339 re-arms recurring jobs wedged in restart-surviving persisted error state. - #88343 reconciles stale process-local in-flight claims against the durable execution ledger. Taken together, however, these fixes reveal the next class boundary: **an old recovery actor can still clear, release, finalize, or re-arm state that now belongs to a newer generation of the same session/job.** The invariant should be: > Every attach, clear, finalize, release, or reconcile operation must identify and conditionally match the exact ownership generation it intends to mutate. A stale actor must be unable to mutate its successor. This issue tracks that class as one coherent recovery/fencing problem rather than another series of incident-local TTL guards. ## 1. `/handoff`: completion-to-cleanup still has a narrow ownership race #88244 adds the session ID to `_handed_off_session_ids` only after the CLI polls `get_handoff_state()` and observes `state == "completed"`. Cleanup suppression is therefore process-local knowledge acquired *after* the gateway has committed the handoff. There is still a legal ordering: 1. Gateway completes the handoff and assumes/reopens the session. 2. CLI has not yet observed `completed`, so its session ID is not yet in `_handed_off_session_ids`. 3. CLI receives SIGTERM / abnormal shutdown / another cleanup trigger. 4. Old CLI finalizes the session now owned by the gateway. That is the original ownership bug compressed into a smaller window. Marking the session as handed off earlier is not sufficient: a failed handoff must leave the CLI as the legitimate owner. The transfer needs a durable generation/lease or equivalent CAS boundary: ```text CLI owns session S generation A Gateway prepares generation B commit atomically transfers A -> B CLI finalize(S, expected_generation=A) succeeds only while A still owns S ``` Cleanup should be rejected by durable ownership state, not by whether this particular CLI process has learned that the transfer completed. ## 2. One-shot dispatch recovery: `clear_run_claim(job_id)` can clear a successor claim #88337 correctly adds cleanup on interpreter-shutdown, execution-creation, and executor-submit failures. But the cleanup primitive is keyed only by `job_id`: ```python def clear_run_claim(job_id: str) -> bool: ... if job.get("run_claim") is not None: job["run_claim"] = None ``` The durable `run_claim` already carries owner/timestamp information. Cleanup does not require that the stored claim still be the claim acquired by the failing attempt. ABA ordering: 1. Attempt A owns claim A. 2. A stalls. 3. A's claim expires/is reclaimed. 4. Attempt B writes claim B for the same job. 5. A resumes into a pre-dispatch failure path. 6. A calls `clear_run_claim(job_id)`. 7. Claim B is erased. B can now be executing while the durable job appears unclaimed, permitting another dispatch. The primitive should be compare-and-clear, preferably against an opaque claim ID plus owner: ```python clear_run_claim( job_id, expected_claim_id=claim_id, expected_owner=owner, ) ``` If the persisted generation changed, stale cleanup is a no-op. ## 3. In-flight ledger reconciliation should match execution identity, not `job_id + claimed_at` #88343 loads the latest execution per job and decides that a terminal row belongs to the process-local claim when its `claimed_at` is at/after `_running_since[job_id]`. That is temporal correlation, not causal identity. A different execution for the same job — manual run, another gateway/process, retry, external provider — can become the latest terminal row and satisfy the timestamp comparison. The local sweeper can then release an unrelated local claim. The inverse exists too: a newer nonterminal execution can become `latest`, hiding the terminal execution belonging to the stale local attempt and delaying recovery until the age path fires. `cron/executions.py` already gives every attempt a unique execution ID. The local running registry should retain that ID and reconcile the exact row: ```text registration_token -> job_id, execution_id, future, monotonic_started_at ``` Then ledger reconciliation is `execution_id -> terminal?`, not "latest row for this job appears new enough". Wall-clock timestamps should remain audit data; they should not be the ownership fence. Local elapsed age should use a monotonic clock. ## 4. The process-local running registry has the same ABA shape `_running_job_ids`, `_running_since`, and `_running_futures` are keyed by job ID. `release_running_job(job_id)` is idempotent but generation-blind. A stale registration can therefore mutate a successor: 1. A registers job X. 2. A stalls before attaching its real future. 3. Sweeper releases X. 4. B registers X. 5. A resumes and attaches A's future to the slot now logically owned by B. 6. A finishes and calls `release_running_job(X)`. 7. B's in-memory protection is removed. The local API needs the same token discipline as the durable claim: ```python token = try_register_running_job(job_id) attach_running_future(job_id, token, future) release_running_job(job_id, token) ``` All three operations must compare the current token. A stale actor must be unable to attach to or release a successor registration. ## 5. Persisted-error recovery needs durable liveness/disposition, not cadence inference alone #88339 detects a restart-surviving wedge from `last_status == "error"`, old `last_run_at`, future `next_run_at`, schedule cadence, and "not running in this process". It then pulls an interval job to `now`, or a cron job to the next legal occurrence. That closes the observed EAGAIN wedge, but the discriminator cannot distinguish a wedge from several legitimate states: - operator intentionally deferred `next_run_at`; - schedule changed after the failed execution; - another process currently owns/retries the job; - the error is permanently blocked (invalid config, revoked credential, missing runtime dependency) rather than retryable; - irregular/DST-sensitive cron cadence is poorly represented by a cached gap between two future occurrences. The cross-process case is the correctness boundary: "not running in this process" is not proof that no live execution exists elsewhere. Recovery should eventually be based on explicit durable state such as: ```text execution_id dispatch_generation lease_owner lease_expiry schedule_revision error_disposition = retryable | blocked | paused ``` Automatic re-arm should require proof that the exact generation has no live owner and is eligible for retry. ## 6. `state.db` degradation is now visible, but not yet self-reconciling #88244 stores the initialization error and sends best-effort recovery guidance to configured home channels. That fixes the silent-failure surface when delivery succeeds. Two remaining sides: 1. The warning itself uses delivery infrastructure that may also be unavailable. If every send fails, the failure can again exist only in logs. 2. The fallback session store is volatile. If `state.db` becomes repairable while the gateway remains alive, there is no demonstrated durable unhealthy latch + retry/reattach + replay/migration path for sessions accepted during degraded operation. At minimum, persistence health should remain durably/probe-visibly degraded until the store is successfully reopened. If volatile sessions cannot safely be migrated, they should be explicitly identified as unrecoverable rather than disappearing on restart. ## 7. `EMFILE` recovery should distinguish temporary headroom from actual healing #88335 correctly makes FD exhaustion a failed tick and retries with backoff. `gc.collect()` and raising the soft `RLIMIT_NOFILE` can create temporary headroom, but neither proves the underlying leak stopped. A live referenced FD leak survives GC; raising the soft limit can simply postpone the next failure. Health should become green only after a real tick successfully acquires the lock and completes the expected tick path. The recovery telemetry should make sustained pressure visible — current descriptor count/limit and/or growth signal if cheaply available — so a limit increase does not erase evidence of a continuing leak. ## Proposed implementation shape This does not need one giant rewrite. The class can be closed incrementally around one shared primitive: **generation-fenced ownership**. ### A. Introduce opaque ownership tokens For each mutable ownership surface: - session lifecycle/handoff generation; - one-shot `run_claim` generation; - process-local running registration token; - exact cron `execution_id`; - external `fire_claim` where not already sufficiently fenced. ### B. Make every destructive transition conditional Replace generation-blind operations with CAS-like forms: - `finalize_session(..., expected_generation=...)` - `clear_run_claim(..., expected_claim_id=...)` - `release_running_job(..., token=...)` - `attach_running_future(..., token=...)` - ledger reconciliation by exact `execution_id` - persisted-error rearm only when durable ownership/disposition proves recovery is safe. ### C. Separate clocks by purpose - monotonic time: in-process elapsed-age/TTL decisions; - durable wall-clock timestamps: audit/history/operator display; - opaque IDs/generations: ownership correctness. No correctness decision should infer ownership from wall-clock ordering when an exact identity can be carried instead. ## Required adversarial tests Please add deterministic interleaving tests, not only steady-state regression tests: - **handoff:** pause after gateway commit but before CLI observes completion; terminate CLI; old generation must not finalize the gateway-owned session; - **durable one-shot claim:** A acquires claim A, B replaces it with claim B, delayed cleanup from A must leave B untouched; - **local running registry:** sweep A, register B, then allow A to attach/release; neither stale operation may mutate B; - **execution reconciliation:** create a terminal execution for the same job in another process after the local claim began; it must not release the unrelated local attempt; - **inverse reconciliation:** newer nonterminal execution must not hide the exact stale execution being reconciled; - **persisted error:** intentionally defer a failed recurring job; automatic recovery must not pull it forward; - **cross-process persisted error:** process B holds a live durable lease while process A scans; A must not re-arm; - **persistence degradation:** all warning transports fail; degraded state remains observable; repair the DB without restart and verify the declared replay/migration policy; - **EMFILE:** keep a live FD leak through GC/limit increase; health stays degraded until an actual successful tick. ## Acceptance criteria - A stale actor cannot clear/release/finalize a newer owner of the same job/session. - Recovery decisions use exact ownership/execution identity wherever that identity exists. - No local running-set mutation is keyed solely by reusable `job_id` when generations can overlap in time. - Cross-process liveness is considered before persisted-error auto-rearm. - Persistence degradation remains observable until durable storage is actually healthy. - The above adversarial interleavings are covered by deterministic tests. ## Why keep this as one class issue The recent fixes are converging on the right semantic direction: cron/session recovery should self-reconcile instead of waiting for TTL, restart, or operator action. The next failure mode is therefore not another missing cleanup call; it is **cleanup without fencing**. Closing this class gives the recovery layer a reusable rule: recovery may revoke only the ownership generation it can prove stale. That rule composes across handoff, cron claims, execution ledger reconciliation, restart recovery, and future multi-process scheduling work.
signal.author: andrexibiza

signal.title: Multiplex: profile identity is late-bound across transport, session, storage, and control paths
signal.text: ## Summary Hermes has accumulated profile isolation at several layers, but it still has no single point where an inbound event's profile identity becomes canonical and immutable **before the first stateful use**. A multiplexed turn can currently have several independently derived identities: 1. **transport / credential owner** — which adapter and bot/account received the event; 2. **routed runtime profile** — which profile's config, SOUL, skills, credentials and filesystem should execute it; 3. **session namespace** — `agent:main:...` versus `agent:<profile>:...`; 4. **physical persistence scope** — which `state.db`, `sessions.json`, logs and auxiliary tables hold the state; 5. **outbound transport** — which live adapter sends the reply, status, approval, typing update or callback. Those answers are currently re-derived at different times from `source.profile`, adapter ownership, transport provenance, `get_active_profile_name()`, the ambient `HERMES_HOME`, or a startup-created store/adapter map. When any one is missing or resolved too early, a single logical turn can split across profiles. The repository now has many concrete reports and PRs repairing individual faces of that same defect class. This issue is the architecture/interlock issue for closing the class rather than landing mutually inconsistent local fixes. ## Scope correction This issue does **not** depend on the claim that equal key strings in two different adapter instances automatically alias their local dictionaries. `_pending_text_batches`, `_active_sessions`, `_session_tasks` and `_post_delivery_callbacks` are adapter-instance state; two adapters each holding the string `agent:main:telegram:dm:<uid>` do not, by that fact alone, share one Python dict entry. The demonstrated defect is stronger and more general: - one adapter can derive `agent:main:...` before its event is stamped and the runner can later derive `agent:<profile>:...` for the same turn; - runner-global and durable lookups can alias profiles that share the same peer tuple; - a correctly routed runtime can persist into the wrong physical store or reply through the wrong transport; - reconstructed, callback, relay, recovery and control-command paths can omit or independently recompute the profile. Any claim of cross-adapter local-map interference should be proven with a real two-adapter behavioral test. The closure contract below does not require that claim. ## Direct interlock map ### A. Identity is established after adapter-level state/key use - #88404 / #88437 — adapter-derived session keys can be built before the per-credential profile handler stamps `source.profile`. - #49634 / #49962 — earlier Telegram manifestation combining late profile stamping and default-adapter egress. - #69156 — independently proposes stamping adapter ownership before busy/approval/session-key checks. - #85350 / #85355 — independently proposes a central `_ensure_source_profile` / `_event_session_key` seam because `/new`, `/reset`, batching and busy paths can key before normal runner ingress. - #80212 — Feishu secondary-profile events can regress to `agent:main` after runtime/reconnect/idle behavior, consistent with profile ownership being lost or rebound too late. These are not four unrelated bugs. They are competing implementations of the same missing invariant: **canonicalize identity before batching, busy state, approval state, commands or session-key construction.** ### B. Interactive and control paths rebuild incomplete identity - #82975 / #82980 — clarify lookup used an unprofiled adapter key while the runner stored the clarify under a profile-namespaced key. - #83345 / #83346 — active-session clarify replies miss the pending clarify and fall into the interrupt path because the adapter and runner use different keys. - #83889 — Feishu production manifestation of the same clarify/key split. - #86308 — Telegram slash-confirm / clarify / dangerous-command callbacks reconstructed a source without applying the routed profile before authorization. - #59018 — Matrix root-DM `/stop` needed profile-aware control-key matching. - #61012 — relay passthrough slash commands, buttons and modals were a second ingress plane that omitted profile even after ordinary relay events carried it. `/stop`, `/new`, `/reset`, clarify, approval buttons and internal redispatch are not secondary consumers. They are session-identity consumers and need the same canonical identity as normal text ingress. ### C. Transport ownership and routed runtime profile are distinct axes The repository already has both halves of this distinction: - #65236 / #65273 / #69246 — for a **shared credential**, a routed secondary runtime has no adapter of its own; egress and intake policy must preserve the receiving transport adapter. - #70620 / #70625 — for a **per-credential** deployment, a routed profile may own a distinct adapter; egress must use that profile's adapter rather than blindly preserving the receiving transport. - #79113 — the inverse route, a secondary-owned adapter routed to `default`, can produce `agent:main` while leaving the tool runtime under the adapter owner's secondary `HERMES_HOME`. - #74787 — `_adapter_for_source` is used by authorization and delivery even though those call sites have opposite fallback requirements. - #87830 — WhatsApp routed-turn authorization demonstrates the same owner/runtime conflation: config belongs to the receiving adapter while `source.profile` names the routed runtime. `source.profile` cannot safely mean both “which profile executes” and “which credential/transport owns this event.” A correct implementation needs both pieces of information and an explicit selection policy for shared-credential and per-credential topologies. ### D. Durable identity, lineage and recovery are independently derived - #74285 — peer fallback omits profile, allowing identical Telegram DM tuples to adopt a sibling profile's session and execute its persona/tools/credentials. - #74153, #74593, #75043 and #85205 — overlapping lookup fences for that report. - #88381 / #88387 — cross-profile adoption can then propagate through parent inheritance and durably mislabel descendants even when the `session_key` remains correct. - #58032 / #58119 / #58136 / #59325 — toggling multiplexing can recover stale rows from another profile namespace. - #75198 — combines profile-scoped peer recovery with another unscoped state key (`/voice`). The durable layer must consume canonical identity. It must not reconstruct profile ownership from a peer tuple that is intentionally identical across bot credentials. ### E. Physical storage policy is currently contradictory This is a merge-blocking architectural interlock: - #87240 describes the multiplexer's **shared session store** as the intended design and changes session listing/detail to read the shared store with profile filters. - #66887, #87723 and #88532 report secondary-profile sessions physically landing in the root/default store as an isolation failure. - #69042 and current #88632 implement the opposite policy: resolve/cache a `SessionDB` per active profile home so secondary writes land in `profiles/<name>/state.db`. Those approaches are mutually exclusive unless the read/write architecture is made explicit. If #87240's reader assumes a shared multiplexer store while #88632 moves writes into per-profile stores, list/detail can diverge in the opposite direction: the reader looks in the shared store while the writer has moved elsewhere. Before either model lands as repository truth, the project needs one declared invariant: - **shared physical store:** every writer uses one store and every reader/filter/API treats `session_key`/`profile_name` as the partition key; or - **per-profile physical stores:** every writer resolves the profile store and aggregation explicitly opens all served profile stores. The current mixture supports neither invariant reliably. ### F. Profile identity is lost on alternate ingress and async boundaries - #60586 — ordinary relay wire events had to carry `profile` explicitly. - #61012 — passthrough interactions required the same change separately. - #68332 — built-in Signal lacked the runner back-reference required to apply `profile_routes` at source construction. - #80956 — A2A request threads lose profile ContextVars; the proposed fix captures immutable adapter-owned security context at startup. - #56508 — import-time path resolution can freeze one profile's hooks directory for every later profile. - #70858 — pairing generation writes the default store while authorization reads the routed profile store. These are the same temporal failure pattern outside session keys: ownership is known at one boundary, discarded, then later inferred from ambient process state. ## Root cause The multiplexer currently treats profile identity as a value that downstream consumers may rediscover rather than as provenance that must be carried. Contributing design problems: 1. `None` is overloaded to mean both **known default profile** and **profile unresolved/not installed**. 2. `source.profile` is overloaded as both logical runtime routing and adapter/credential ownership. 3. Key construction is a free function used directly by adapters and subsystems, so callers can omit the profile or choose different fallback rules. 4. Some stateful objects (`SessionStore`, `SessionDB`, caches, path constants) bind to the ambient profile at construction/import time, before per-turn scope exists. 5. Interactive, synthetic, relay and recovery paths rebuild `SessionSource` independently and do not all preserve the same provenance. 6. Authorization and delivery share adapter-resolution helpers despite requiring different fail-closed/fallback behavior. ## Required invariants for class closure ### 1. Canonical identity before stateful use Before any of the following occurs, Hermes must have one canonical identity for the event: - text/photo/media batching; - active/busy session guards and pending-message queues; - `/stop`, `/new`, `/reset`, clarify and approval/callback resolution; - internal `gateway_session_key` validation and redispatch; - session lookup, creation, recovery, reset and parent inheritance; - physical store selection; - status/progress/typing/final response delivery. A frozen `SessionIdentity`/`RoutingIdentity` value object would make the contract explicit, but the exact API is open. It should at minimum carry: - transport binding / receiving adapter provenance; - credential-owner profile or account identity; - routed runtime profile; - normalized session namespace; - persistence scope/store identity. ### 2. `default` must be explicit internally Known ownership by the default profile should remain the string/value `default` internally. `None` should mean absent or unresolved. The serializer may still emit legacy `agent:main:...` byte-for-byte. In multiplex mode, an unresolved identity at a stateful boundary should fail closed or be deterministically resolved at the canonicalization seam. It should not silently become default ownership. ### 3. Separate transport owner from runtime profile The routing decision matrix needs to be explicit: | Topology | Runtime/profile state | Intake policy | Egress transport | |---|---|---|---| | Per-credential profile, no route override | credential owner | owner adapter | owner adapter | | Shared credential routed to secondary | routed profile | receiving transport owner | receiving transport | | Per-credential source routed to another profile that owns an adapter | routed profile | receiving transport policy unless explicitly delegated | declared routed adapter policy | | Secondary-owned transport routed to `default` | default | receiving transport policy | receiving transport unless product policy says otherwise | | Restored/synthetic source with no live provenance | stored runtime profile | fail closed unless an explicit binding can be resolved | fail closed; never guess another bot | The exact product choice for the two route-override rows should be documented and tested. What must not happen is accidental selection by whichever field a helper happens to inspect first. ### 4. One session-key construction seam Adapter and plugin code should not call the free `build_session_key(source, ...)` path directly with optional/omitted profile semantics. A gateway/adapter-owned constructor should consume the canonical identity. Add a repository test or lint check preventing new adapter-level direct key construction outside the canonical module/seam. Otherwise this class will recur with the next platform adapter. ### 5. One storage model Resolve the #87240 versus #88632 policy conflict before merging both assumptions. Whichever model is selected must make these agree: - session key namespace; - `profile_name` column; - physical DB path; - `sessions.json` / routing index; - list/count/detail/search APIs; - parent lineage; - topic/voice/auxiliary state. ### 6. Canonical identity survives every boundary Serialization/reconstruction must preserve the necessary fields across: - relay ordinary events and passthrough interactions; - inline callbacks; - held-inbound redispatch and reconnect; - internal events, Kanban wakeups and webhook/API ingress; - session recovery and restart; - thread/executor boundaries where ContextVars do not propagate. Ambient `get_active_profile_name()` or process-global environment must be fallback-only when no canonical identity exists, never an override of carried provenance. ## Acceptance matrix Class closure needs composed behavioral tests, not only helper-string tests. ### Per-credential collision case Two profiles, two Telegram bot tokens, the same human DMing both bots (`chat.id == user.id`): - distinct canonical session namespaces; - no cross-profile session adoption or parent inheritance; - correct physical persistence according to the selected storage model; - correct bot for progress, typing, approval, streamed and final replies; - `/stop`, `/new`, `/reset`, clarify and approval on bot A cannot affect bot B; - reconnect and idle eviction do not erase adapter ownership. ### Shared-credential routed case One live adapter, route one chat/thread to a secondary profile: - runtime/config/SOUL/tools/session namespace are secondary; - intake policy and egress use the shared receiving transport; - no requirement for a secondary adapter registry entry; - callbacks and synthetic/internal events preserve the routed profile. ### Secondary-to-default inverse case A secondary-owned adapter with a route target of `default`: - session key is legacy `agent:main:...`; - runtime `HERMES_HOME`, credentials and tools are default; - transport provenance remains explicit and egress follows the documented policy; - persistence lands in the store selected for default under the chosen storage architecture. ### Recovery and alternate ingress Run the same assertions after: - gateway restart; - routing-index miss / conservative peer fallback; - idle-TTL eviction; - adapter reconnect; - relay normal event and passthrough callback; - inline approval/clarify callback; - internally routed event carrying `gateway_session_key`. ### Composed-head interlocks At minimum, test the combined behavior represented by: - #88437 with #83346 — #83346 deliberately assumes the adapter busy key stays `agent:main`; #88437 changes that premise. - #88437 with #85355/#69156 — choose or reconcile the competing ingress canonicalization mechanisms rather than stacking duplicate state. - #88387 with the selected peer-fallback implementation and storage model. - #87240 with #88632 — do not merge contradictory reader/writer storage assumptions. - #69246 with #70625 — shared transport and per-credential override must both remain correct. ## Existing-data repair Forward-only fixes are insufficient for deployments that already crossed profiles. Add a dry-run + repair path that can detect and optionally repair: - `session_key` namespace versus `profile_name` mismatch; - rows physically stored in a DB inconsistent with the selected storage model; - cross-namespace `parent_session_id` links; - duplicate/cross-profile `gateway_routing` entries; - profile-less Telegram topic/voice rows; - stale `sessions.json` entries that re-seed wrong routing on boot. The repair should report every proposed move/update before mutation and preserve a backup/rollback artifact. ## Architectural precedent #67455's multi-account Telegram design states the useful invariant directly: account identity is stamped on the source and key construction reads it from the source so the adapter guard and session store cannot derive different identities for the same event. Multiplex profiles need the same construction, generalized to transport owner + routed runtime profile rather than one overloaded field. ## Non-goals - This is not a request to merge every linked PR. - This does not require changing the public legacy `agent:main` key format. - This does not claim every profile-scoped config/cache bug belongs in one implementation PR. - This does not choose shared-store versus per-profile-store policy; it requires that the repository choose one and make readers/writers consistent. ## Proposed disposition of current work 1. Treat #88437, #85355 and #69156 as competing/overlapping ingress implementations and select one canonical seam. 2. Rebase/retest #83346 after that seam because its regression fixture encodes the old adapter-key premise. 3. Choose the physical storage model before landing both #87240 and #88632 assumptions. 4. Land one peer-fallback fence, then retain #88387's inheritance fence and add repair for existing crossed lineages. 5. Compose #69246 and #70625 into one documented transport-selection matrix. 6. Add the end-to-end matrix above before declaring the multiplex profile-isolation class closed.

signal.title: fix(voice): global playback arbitration — one sound at a time across sessions
signal.text: ## Summary Fix the TTS **audio-stacking (叠音)** bug: concurrent playback requests from different sessions/windows/processes could run **multiple `afplay` streams at once**, because `play_audio_file()` stored the current player in a global reference but a new request never interrupted the previous one — it just overwrote the reference. **One sound at a time, everywhere.** Latest request wins (barge-in), matching the existing `stop_playback()` semantics. ## Problem - Hermes Desktop renders multiple sessions against one backend `serve` process; a separate `gateway` process may run alongside. - `play_audio_file()` spawns a system player (`afplay` on macOS) and records it in the module-global `_active_playback` under `_playback_lock`. - A second concurrent request **overwrote** the reference instead of interrupting the first player → both players ran → audio layering. - The renderer's sequence guard (`voice-playback.ts`) ran only **after** backend playback had already started → couldn't prevent the overlap. **Repro:** two sessions hit read-aloud within ~100ms → two `afplay` processes coexist → 叠音. ## Fix (3 parts) 1. **In-process arbitration** — before spawning any player, atomically (under `_playback_lock`) terminate the previous `_active_playback`, bounded-wait (0.5s) for it to exit, then spawn + record the new one. `proc.wait()` stays outside the lock so `stop_playback()` can still interrupt mid-play. 2. **Cross-process arbitration** — a shared pidfile `HERMES_HOME/tts/.audio-playback.pid` records the current player. Before spawning, `_interrupt_other_process_playback()` reads it, verifies the PID still names a system audio player (`ps -p <pid> -o comm=` — guards against **PID reuse killing an unrelated process**), terminates it, and waits for exit. The new player records its own PID; ownership-checked `_clear_playback_pid()` removes it on completion or stop. 3. **No fall-through after interrupt** — a superseded (`was_current=False`) or signal-killed (`rc < 0`) player returns `False` instead of falling through to the next player in the list (`afplay → ffplay → aplay`). Re-spawning would re-layer the very stream we were interrupted on and defeat the arbitration. ## Behavior contract - One sound at a time **per process** and **across processes** sharing `HERMES_HOME`. - Latest request wins (barge-in); the interrupted call reports `False`. - `stop_playback()` (`/api/audio/stop`) still works and clears both the in-process slot and the pidfile. - Normal completion reports `True`; the pidfile is removed only by its owner. - No credential change — existing `hermes_subprocess_env(inherit_credentials=False)` scrub unchanged; players never inherit gateway tokens/API keys. - Best-effort: `ps`/file failures are swallowed — playback never blocks on arbitration. ## Why a pidfile and not flock / a daemon? | Option | Verdict | |--------|---------| | **PID file + verified-comm kill** | ~60 LOC, no new infra, PID-reuse guard, works across unrelated processes | | `flock` (blocking) | Queue semantics — a hung player blocks everyone; can't *interrupt* | | Unified audio daemon | Cleanest but a new long-running service — disproportionate for playback | See `docs/security/DECISION-RECORD-tts-playback-arbitration.md`. ## Security design The only privileged primitive (cross-process `SIGTERM`) is gated behind a verified-comm allowlist (`afplay`/`ffplay`/`aplay`); pidfile content is int-parse guarded (`pid <= 0` short-circuits); kill+spawn is atomic under the non-reentrant lock (no nested `stop_playback()` call → no deadlock); all player spawns keep the pre-existing credential scrub. Full audit: `docs/security/SECURITY-AUDIT-tts-playback-arbitration.md` Baseline: `docs/security/SECURITY-BASELINE-tts-playback-arbitration.md` ## Self-test (macOS, M5 Max) - **New tests** — `TestPlaybackArbitration` (3) + `TestCrossProcessArbitration` (4): **7/7 pass**. - **Full suite** — 63 passed; 3 pre-existing environment-only failures (sounddevice beep test + 2 WSL-only tests); **zero regression** vs baseline (57 passed / 3 failed before the change). - **Real concurrent plays** (2 threads, 4s+2s WAVs) — `afplay` peak = 1; first call interrupted, second completes. - **Real cross-process plays** (2 independent Python processes) — first process's player interrupted by the second; `afplay` peak = 1; no residue; pidfile cleaned. ## Who should enable No opt-in needed — this is a bug fix for everyone who uses TTS playback (desktop read-aloud, voice-conversation mode, CLI/TUI voice, gateway audio). The pidfile path is derived from `HERMES_HOME`; nothing to configure. ## Platform compatibility - **macOS** — primary target (`afplay` path), fully tested. - **Linux / WSL** — same code path (`ffplay`/`aplay` + PowerShell fallback); the arbitration guards are platform-neutral; WSL-specific tests unaffected. - **Windows** — system-player list is empty there; `play_audio_file` already falls through; arbitration adds no new platform calls (`ps` is only invoked on POSIX; on Windows the comm check fails closed → no cross-process kill). ## Quick-start Nothing to do — restart the backend and the fix is live. To observe it: ```bash # Terminal 1 — long playback afplay -t 5 /path/to/a.wav & # or any Hermes read-aloud # Terminal 2 — new playback interrupts it afplay /path/to/b.wav # Hermes: a second session's read-aloud ``` Only the newest sound is heard; the old one stops within ~50ms. ## Troubleshooting | Symptom | Cause | Fix | |---------|-------|-----| | Two sounds still overlap | Backend not restarted after upgrade | Restart `serve`/desktop; both processes must run the new code | | No sound at all | `afplay` missing / no output device | Pre-existing behavior unchanged; check `which afplay` | | Stale `tts/.audio-playback.pid` | Process crashed mid-play | Harmless — next play verifies the PID via `ps`, fails closed, overwrites | | Cross-process kill not happening | `ps` unavailable (non-POSIX) | Fails closed by design (no kill); in-process arbitration still applies |

signal.title: [Bug] Windows/Chinese file delivery & preview: garbled MEDIA filenames, artifact-tag chain broken on Windows paths, dismiss not persisted
signal.text: **Environment**: Windows 11, Hermes Agent v0.20.0 (2026.8.3, main @ f4c2c263f), Chinese locale, CJK paths (e.g. `D:\坚果云同步\工作\...`) Three related desktop-UX defects, all from **POSIX-path / ASCII-filename assumptions**. Real daily impact for Chinese/Windows users. ## 1. MEDIA attachment filename shows URL-encoded garbage for CJK paths - `mediaName()` (media.ts) uses `new URL(path).pathname` — WHATWG `URL.pathname` always percent-encodes CJK → filename displays as `%E6%B5%8B...` in the attachment card. - File opens fine; display-only defect. ASCII filenames unaffected (why English-only users never see it). - Current workaround: copy to ASCII-named path before delivery. ## 2. Composer status-stack artifact tag chain broken for Windows paths - `looksLikePath()` (targets.ts) accepts only `file://`, `/`, `./`, `~/` prefixes — `C:\...` (backslash) never matches → **no artifact tag at all** for Windows absolute paths. - macOS agents naturally write `/Users/...` → tag + IPC preview work (Claude-style artifact). Windows agents write `C:\...` → nothing. - Even with POSIX form (`/c/Users/...`), IPC `normalizePreviewTarget` resolves it to non-existent `C:\c\...` → tag appears but preview fails. - Verified 2026-08-13: `write_file(path="/c/Users/...test.html")` → tag shows, click preview fails; `write_file(path="C:\...")` → no tag. ## 3. Preview-artifact tag dismiss not persisted — tags keep returning - `dismissPreviewArtifact` (preview-status.ts) removes only from an in-memory atom; the tool row's `useEffect` re-registers on every remount (scroll / window re-open) → dismissed tags reappear. `/clear` doesn't help; only `/new` clears. - Users constantly hit this with generated HTML reports. **Expected**: (1) decode CJK filenames for display; (2) accept `C:\` absolute paths in `looksLikePath` / `localPreviewTarget` (e.g. `/^[a-zA-Z]:[\\/]/`); (3) persist dismissed-artifact state per session. **Related**: #84986 (file actions on preview links); #84375 (same POSIX-assumption class in search_files — fixed 2026-08-12, thanks).

signal.title: Required CI aggregate treats skipped and non-failure states as passing and excludes Docker from the gate
signal.text: <!-- security-campaign-marker: SECURITY-AUDIT-42-CLASSES-F51AA6A9 --> <!-- security-campaign-class: SECURITY-CLASS-7f244fef4359b8ad --> **Campaign interlock:** Part of [EPIC #82591](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/issues/82591). **Final class:** `SECURITY-CLASS-7f244fef4359b8ad` **Consensus contract:** `R5-C-004` # Required CI aggregate treats skipped and non-failure states as passing and excludes Docker from the gate **Consensus contract:** `R5-C-004` **Source pin:** `f51aa6a9b5ce514e15f8e337777f522fd5cc6fa2` **Route:** public hardening issue under `SECURITY.md` §3.2 **Severity:** `HIGH` ## Scope - `.github/workflows/ci.yml:190-250` (blob `6aa601e264fe854f532b72358343c55dd33e58be`) - `.github/workflows/ci.yml:107-123` (blob `6aa601e264fe854f532b72358343c55dd33e58be`) - `.github/workflows/ci.yml:219-222` (blob `6aa601e264fe854f532b72358343c55dd33e58be`) ## Defect class The confirmed source defect is the aggregate's result semantics and explicit coverage exclusions; it is not a claim that GitHub branch protection currently requires or accepts a particular check configuration. ## Current controls - Job result visibility in the summary. - Explicit workflow dependencies and timeouts. - Some empty-output paths fail closed outside this evaluator. ## Required remediation - Require result == success except for an exact, independently justified skip. - Reject cancelled/timed_out/neutral/missing/unknown states. - Separate intentional OS skips from classifier skips and make Docker/release-sensitive checks required for matching changes. ## Acceptance contract - Unit-test the evaluator for success, failure, skipped, cancelled, timed_out, neutral, missing, and unknown states; only explicit success or justified skip may pass. - Make a changed desktop path require E2E and a Docker-sensitive path require the Docker status. - Add an uncovered-change invariant and fail when any changed file maps to no lane. ## Affected files - `.github/workflows/ci.yml` - `scripts/ci/classify_changes.py` ## Godfile dependencies - `CI aggregate evaluator` - `conditional job selectors` - `branch-protection required-check contract` Any touched file above 2,000 lines must route through a separate behavior-neutral Shard before the hardening change. The security PR must not grow or restore a godfile. ## Existing graph and credit - No overlap recorded ## Interlock Part of #82591. The implementation PR must use a closing keyword for this issue, and both the issue and EPIC must link back to the exact PR. ## Evidence boundary This issue contains the independently adjudicated hardening contract, not a public exploit recipe. signal.title: MCP write-capable tools no longer risk duplicate side effects on mid-flight session expiry (port cloudflare-os#168)
signal.text: ## Summary A write-capable MCP tool call that fails with a session-expired/transport error is no longer auto-retried — the request may already have executed server-side, and a blind retry risks a duplicate side effect MCP offers no way to undo. Ported from cloudflare/cloudflare-os#168 ("Harden MCP connection lifecycle"). Root cause of the risk: our `_SESSION_EXPIRED_MARKERS` classifier matches both genuine pre-dispatch rejections ("session not found") AND failure shapes that routinely fire *after* dispatch — `ClosedResourceError`, "broken pipe", "connection closed" mid-response, or a proxy-synthesized session-404 after the upstream accepted the request. The previous recovery path (`_handle_session_expired_and_retry`) re-ran every tool call once regardless. ## Changes - `tools/mcp_tool.py`: `_handle_session_expired_and_retry` gains keyword-only `call_may_have_side_effects`. When True it still heals the transport (reconnect + breaker reset on success) but never re-runs the call; instead it returns a structured `outcome_unknown=True` tool error telling the model to verify with a read before re-invoking. - `tools/mcp_tool.py`: new `_tool_is_read_only(server, tool)` helper — reuses the discovery-time `readOnlyHint` capture the trust gate already maintains. Fails safe: missing/unknown/malformed annotations classify as write-capable. - `tools/mcp_tool.py`: the `tools/call` handler passes `call_may_have_side_effects=not _tool_is_read_only(...)`. The four read-only handlers (resources/list, resources/read, prompts/list, prompts/get) keep unconditional retry — they are protocol-level reads. - The OAuth-401 path keeps its retry for all tools: a 401 means the server demanded authorization before dispatch, so the call never executed (matches upstream's `McpAuthRequiredError` → safe-to-retry rule). - `tests/tools/test_mcp_tool_session_expired.py`: 4 new tests (write not retried + outcome_unknown, read-only still retries, fail-safe classification, direct helper coverage); existing retry tests updated to register `readOnlyHint=True` since unannotated tools no longer auto-retry. ## Adaptation notes Upstream models this as `callMayHaveTakenEffect(err)` over typed error classes (`McpCallNotDispatchedError` → safe, `McpSessionExpiredError` → unsafe for writes since a fronting proxy can synthesize it post-dispatch). Hermes' classifier is string/type-marker based with no dispatch-boundary signal, so the port keys the decision on the tool's write-capability instead — the same fail-safe direction ("anything not positively known safe is treated as possibly performed"), wired into the `readOnlyHint` metadata we already capture for trust-tier gating. No toolset/schema mutation; prompt caching unaffected. Complementary to open PR #84931 (durable tool-attempt identity in `_meta` so governed servers can dedupe); this PR removes the client-side duplicate dispatch for ordinary servers. ## Validation | | Before | After | |---|---|---| | Write tool, session expires mid-flight | silently re-dispatched (possible double side effect) | 1 dispatch, transport healed, `outcome_unknown` error returned | | Read-only tool (`readOnlyHint: true`), session expired | retry once | retry once (unchanged) | | resources/prompts handlers | retry once | retry once (unchanged) | | OAuth 401 on any tool | recover + retry once | recover + retry once (unchanged) | Tests: `tests/tools/test_mcp_tool_session_expired.py` + `test_mcp_trust_gating.py` → 28/28; broader MCP subset (tool, 401, circuit breaker, reconnect signal/reset, transport group, failure classification, connect/shutdown, issue-948) → 138/138. Source: https://github.com/cloudflare/cloudflare-os/pull/168 ## Infographic ![MCP Writes: At Most Once](https://v3b.fal.media/files/b/0aa6c51f/215vdKEGKPwJ8CY4kuwvR_kDLgLmfV.png)

signal.text: <!-- security-campaign-marker: SECURITY-AUDIT-42-CLASSES-F51AA6A9 --> <!-- security-campaign-class: SECURITY-CLASS-bf89e9b049acb1d6 --> **Campaign interlock:** Part of [EPIC #82591](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/issues/82591). **Final class:** `SECURITY-CLASS-bf89e9b049acb1d6` **Consensus contract:** `R3-C-004` # Default URL redaction preserves userinfo and query credentials at non-navigation-capable boundaries **Consensus contract:** `R3-C-004` **Source pin:** `f51aa6a9b5ce514e15f8e337777f522fd5cc6fa2` **Route:** public hardening issue under `SECURITY.md` §3.2 **Severity:** `HIGH` ## Scope - `agent/redact.py:963-992` (blob `b5dca332c4ade1cee8564a02e22f8b9d10f750b9`) - `agent/auxiliary_client.py:6253-6292` (blob `13bce3f884199c96fcfba0b760860af1b031f6c9`) ## Defect class Confirmed policy-context mismatch: navigation-safe preservation is reused at log/provider-metadata boundaries. signal.title: fix(relay): unwrap lazy completed streams
signal.text: ## What does this PR do? Correctly unwraps a completed provider response when Relay defers a nominal streaming callback until the first pull. A genuine first stream chunk is prefetched and returned normally; a completed response is surfaced directly and its stream resources are closed. Some provider adapters ignore `stream=True` and return a completed response. On the managed path Relay starts the callback lazily, so Hermes previously checked `final_response` before the callback ran and returned an apparently empty stream. This focused fix is extracted from #77915 and ported onto current `main` while preserving its newer stream-cleanup and operation-lease behavior. #77915 will drop the duplicated commits after this lands. ## Related Issue Relates to #77915 ## Type of Change - [x] 🐛 Bug fix (non-breaking change that fixes an issue) - [ ] ✨ New feature (non-breaking change that adds functionality) - [ ] 🔒 Security fix - [ ] 📝 Documentation update - [x] ✅ Tests (adding or improving test coverage) - [ ] ♻️ Refactor (no behavior change) - [ ] 🎯 New skill (bundled or hub) ## Changes Made - Prime one lazy managed-stream step before deciding whether the result is streaming or complete. - Buffer and preserve a genuine first chunk. - Clear prefetched chunks during close and finish completed responses during priming. - Add regressions for lazy completed responses and real iterators. ## How to Test 1. Run the lazy completed-response tests in `tests/agent/test_relay_llm.py`. 2. Verify a genuine stream still returns its first prefetched chunk. 3. Run Ruff on `agent/relay_llm.py` and its tests. ## Checklist ### Code - [x] I've read the [Contributing Guide](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) - [x] My commit messages follow [Conventional Commits](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) (`fix(scope):`, `feat(scope):`, etc.) - [x] I searched for [existing PRs](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/pulls) to make sure this isn't a duplicate - [x] My PR contains **only** changes related to this fix/feature (no unrelated commits) - [ ] I've run `pytest tests/ -q` and all tests pass - [x] I've added tests for my changes (required for bug fixes, strongly encouraged for features) - [x] I've tested on my platform: macOS arm64 ### Documentation & Housekeeping - [x] I've updated relevant documentation (README, `docs/`, docstrings) — N/A - [x] I've updated `cli-config.yaml.example` if I added/changed config keys — N/A - [x] I've updated `CONTRIBUTING.md` or `AGENTS.md` if I changed architecture or workflows — N/A - [x] I've considered cross-platform impact (Windows, macOS) per the [compatibility guide](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#cross-platform-compatibility) — pure Python iterator lifecycle - [x] I've updated tool descriptions/schemas if I changed tool behavior — N/A ## Screenshots / Logs Three focused completed-response and iterator regressions passed. Ruff passed on all changed files.

signal.title: Hermes Agent v0.20.3 (2026.8.16.2)
signal.text: # Hermes Agent v0.20.3 (v2026.8.16.2) **Release Date:** August 16, 2026 > Patch release. This tag rolls up the ~125 PRs merged since v0.20.2 into a stable tagged release for downstream consumers (Docker images, hosted deployments, fresh installs). --- ## About this release Since v0.20.2 (v2026.8.16, tagged earlier today), this window landed **~250 commits** across **~461 files** (+42,613 / −1,641) — **~125 merged PRs** including the MCP 2.x SDK migration and 2026-07-28 stateless protocol support, the bundled Bot Mode (hermes-bots) plugin with the core teammate protocol, the CommandCode provider plugin, subprocess Python runtime ownership hardening (PYTHONHOME/PYTHONPATH isolation), Cua Driver 0.20 runtime contracts for computer use, kanban worktree/dispatch fixes, cron continuity flags, desktop remote-gateway headers and connection self-healing, cron scheduler self-heal (EMFILE recovery, stale-claim reconciliation, wedged-job re-arm), session handoff data-loss fixes, plus a wave of ports from the ecosystem scout slate (plugin install security scanning, /worktree, /rollback hand-edit preservation, UTF-16 file reads, Gemini 3 tool-call ID preservation, and more). **Full curated release notes for this window will ship with v0.21.0**, which will document everything from v0.20.0 onward — highlights, feature areas, and complete contributor credits. Nothing in this window is skipped. ## Updating - `hermes update` from an existing install - Fresh install: `curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/main/scripts/install.sh | bash` **Full Changelog**: https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/compare/v2026.8.16...v2026.8.16.2
